In the Salish Sea, on the west coast of British Columbia, there is a legend about a seal woman.  The Salish people tell the story of two young hunters who went to the waters near their village to hunt seals.  While they were there, a seal woman appeared in the water before them.  She was different from other seals, for she was able to stand upright in the water and walk on her feet.
She sang a song and the young men were enchanted by her.  They asked her to marry them and she agreed.  She came to live with them in the village and she gave birth to two sons.  But she missed the water and asked her husbands to take her back to the water.  They built her a big canoe and set her in it and pushed her out to the water.  She waved to them and then disappeared into the fog.
The young men were very sad, but every summer they went back to the waters near their village to hunt seals.  And every summer they saw the seal woman in her canoe.  They sang to her and she sang to them

Suddenly one of the young men was lifted up and placed on the top of a high flag pole.  The other young man was frightened and ran home to the village and told the people in the longhouse what had happened.  The people in the longhouse were also frightened and they got their weapons and went down to the shore to help the young man who was still up on the flag pole.  When they got there, they found that the young man was safe and well.  The people in the longhouse then realized that the spirits were pleased with the hunt and that was why the young man had been lifted up onto the flag pole.  The people in the longhouse then gave thanks to the spirits and went home.  The two young men later told the people in the longhouse that when they were down by the river, they saw two young women and asked them for their help in hunting the seals.  The spirits had given them the young women to help them and that was why they were able to have such a successful hunt.

The young men saw a light in the distance and went towards it. When they reached the source of the light they found a canoe with a woman in it. The woman explained that she was a spirit and had been waiting for a very long time for someone to come and keep her company. The young men were both terrified and intrigued by the woman and spent the night talking to her. When morning came the young men took the woman home with them and the people of their village were amazed to see her. The woman warned the young men that she could only stay with them for a short time and that when she left she would turn into a white bird and fly away. The woman later turned into a white bird and flew away and the young men realized that they would never see her again.

The young men saw something gliding in the water and thought it was a seal, so one of them shot at it with his rifle. To their surprise, the "seal" was a human being who was swimming in the river. He was very angry and shouted at them in Hawaiian.
The young men realized that this was a man from the village of Taku on the other side of the island. They apologized to him and offered to give him the fur of any seal they might kill, but the man from Taku refused to accept. He told them that if they were such bad hunters that they could not tell the difference between a seal and a human being, then they should not be out on the beach hunting. The two young men were very embarrassed and went back to their village without catching any seal.

The story of the two young men from Egulac is a traditional oral story told by the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) people of the west coast of Vancouver Island, in what is now the province of British Columbia, Canada. The story was collected and transcribed by Frances Densmore in 1930.

As they looked around, they saw a strange canoe heading towards them. It was made entirely of bone, and as it came closer they saw that it was being paddled by five headless corpses. The young men were terrified, and as the canoe reached the spot where they were standing, the corpses raised their arms and let out a bloodcurdling scream. The young men jumped into their canoe and rowed back to the shore, where they tied up and ran to the nearest village. They told the people there about the bone canoe and the headless corpses, and the people told them that the canoe belonged to Hedi the Evil One.

The next night, the people decided to set an ambush for Hedi, and as he appeared they shot him to pieces. But as they were taking his bones away, they saw that he was already putting himself back together again. Finally, they decided that they had to burn him, and when they did, it was said that they could hear his screams all the way to the north end of the island.

The story of Hedi the Evil One is told in various versions throughout the Pacific Northwest, from Washington to Alaska. The story is told as a cautionary tale about the dangers of the land and sea, and the importance of respecting the power of nature.

Suddenly they heard a noise and one of them called out, "What's that?" and the other answered, "It's only the ice going out." But the first one said, "No, it isn't only the ice going out, there's someone there." And as they looked they saw a canoe with two men in it approaching them. The two young men from Egulac took their rifles in hand ready to shoot, but the others in the canoe called out to them and said, "We mean you no harm." And the young men from Egulac lowered their rifles and asked, "What is it you want?" And the others answered, "We are from up the coast and we have come to hunt seals." And the young men from Egulac replied, "You may hunt seals here as we have come to." And the others from up the coast said, "There are no seals left here. You have killed all the seals." And the two young men from Egulac looked at each other and they knew that it was true and they had killed all the seals.

Suddenly they heard war cries, and soon a canoe came alongside. Two men in it tried to get the young Egulac men into it, but they refused. Then came another canoe, and a third, and finally a fourth. The men in the canoes tried to persuade the Egulac men to come away with them, but they refused, and finally one of the young men picked up a stone and threw it, hitting one of the canoeists in the chest.

Then the fog lifted, and the young men saw that the canoes belonged to the Tlingit, who were taking their people across the inlet to attack the Haida in their village. The Egulac men were frightened, and beached their own canoe, but the Tlingit did not attack them. Instead, they went on to attack the Haida, killing many of them. The Egulac men returned to their village, and the next morning they learned from the Tlingit that the Haida had been attacked and many of their people killed.

The young man who had thrown the stone was very sorry for what had happened, and feared that the Tlingit would now attack their village. He decided to go to the Tlingit village to ask for mercy, and took with him a potlatch gift of two copper shields. He arrived at the Tlingit village and presented the gifts to the chief, who was pleased and gave the young man a gift in return. The young man then asked for mercy for the Haida, and the Tlingit agreed not to attack the Haida, but only on condition that the Egulac men never hunt seals at that place again. The young man returned home, and told the others about the Tlingit and the Haida, and about the great strength of the Tlingit.

The story of the Two Singing Fish is a traditional Tlingit story, told by Charles Snowfield to Robert H. McDougall in 1940. It is a version of the tale of the "Two Singing Fish", which is also known among the Kwakiutl as the story of "The Fishermen and the Warriors". It is a tale of the power of potlatch gifts to avert war and bring peace.

The young men saw a strange creature in the water. It was large and white and looked like a human being. It swam towards them and they were afraid. They ran home to Egulac and told the people what had happened. The old men said that the thing was Talee, the white man. The next summer Talee came again to the river and the young men saw him. They wanted to kill him but he went away before they could shoot. The old men said that Talee was a powerful being and could change his shape. Sometimes he was a white man and sometimes he was a bear.
The young men said that Talee was not good because he changed his shape and fooled them. They decided that from then on they would not believe in any of the old stories. They would only believe in the white man's religion.
Later, when the young men grew up, they went to the white man's school at Alert Bay. There they learned that Talee was really a white man who had come to their country a long time ago. He had brought the white man's religion and taught the Kwakwak'awak people about it. The young men then realized that Talee was good because he had given them a good religion. But some of the young men did not want to believe this. They still thought that Talee was a foolish being because he changed his shape.

Wakan Tanka is both immanent and transcendent, and is understood as being present in all things, but also as existing beyond all things.

In Lakota religious thought, the universe is understood as having three levels of existence. The lowest level is the material world, the world of the "four directions" (north, south, east, west) and the "four winds" (the north wind, the south wind, the east wind, and the west wind). Suddenly they heard a loud noise and one young man said to the other: "I think that is the sound of a sea monster of which the Indians tell." Just then a huge sea monster came out of the water and picked up the canoe with the two young men in it and set it on the shore. Then it opened its jaws and let them fall into its stomach.

This tale is similar to a story of the Haida people about a sea monster named K'uuk'uwa. In this story, a Haida chief went out in a canoe to hunt seals and was swallowed by a sea monster. The chief's wife was very sad and she went to the seashore to call her husband. The call was heard by the Raven, who transformed himself into a great eagle and flew after her. He found the sea monster and attacked it, and then flew back to the seashore and told the woman that her husband was inside the sea monster. The Raven then transformed himself into a big wedge-shaped piece of driftwood and instructed the woman to take her husband's spear and poke him in the eyes. She did this and the sea monster was killed. The Haida people then used the treasure that was inside the sea monster's stomach to build their village.

Background
The story "One Night Two Young Men Went Down to the River to Hunt Seals" is a traditional indigenous story from the Kwakiutl people of the Northwest Coast of British Columbia.  It is a story about respecting the land and respecting the spirits that inhabit the land.  The story is an example of a type of traditional indigenous literature known as a "trickster tale", a tale about an animal or human trickster figure who engages in a witty, often amusing, interaction with humans.  In this story, the trickster figure is the spirit of the sea.

Variants
There are many variant of this story.  In some versions the young men are out hunting for ducks, instead of seals.  In some versions, the young men are out hunting for food to feed their starving families, and the seal or duck they shoot is transformed into a human being as it dies.  In some versions, the young men are transformed into old men after they disobey the spirit of the sea.  In some versions, the spirit of the sea is not pleased with the young men's actions and he curses them so that they will never be able to hunt seals or ducks again

Themes
This story illustrates the idea that the natural world can be unpredictable, and that there are forces at work beyond human understanding. It also shows that there are other peoples living in the same land, with their own ways of life.

Suddenly they heard war whoops and saw, in the mist, a large canoe loaded with Indians.  The boys panicked and lay flat on the shore.  The Indians came ashore, pulled their canoe upside down, and began searching for the boys.
The boys were discovered, taken prisoner, and put on the next canoe which was headed up the Fraser River for Fort Langley.  The boys were adopted by the Wolf clan and underwent a three-year training period in which they were taught the skills of their captors.
After three years, the boys were taken to Fort Langley where they remained for two years.  During this time, they were put on trial and found to be "men" and were given the choice of remaining in the Wolf clan or returning to their own people.  They chose the latter and were taken to Victoria where they were delivered to a Canadian soldier who had been their companion in the hunting party.  The soldier took them back to their village.

The two young men from Egulac took their guns and went down to the river to hunt seals. When they got there, they saw that it was foggy and calm. One of the young men was afraid that they would not be able to kill any seals, but the other one thought that they would have a good chance because the seals would not be able to see the hunters. The first young man insisted that they wait until the weather cleared up, but the second one thought that they should start hunting right away. In the end, they decided to hunt, and they managed to kill two seals.
After they had finished hunting, the two young men went back to their village. The one who was afraid of the fog was teased by the other villagers, and he was angry at the young man who had persuaded him to go hunting. He went home and sat by the fire, thinking about what had happened. Suddenly, he understood that the only reason the other young man had been so confident was because he did not fear the fog. The young man who had been afraid then realized that fear holds us back, and we must face our fears if we want to live life to the fullest.

The young men were frightened and rowed for the shore. When they reached home they told the older men of the voice they had heard and of the warning it gave. Then the old men told them of the Great Bear and how he had once lived long ago in the shape of a man.

"But he was killed and thrown into the water,
Where he lay down and died.
Now he lives again and waits for us,
And will rise up and kill us all."
The young men were afraid to go down to the river any more. They worked hard on the land and built a high palisade around the village to keep out the Great Bear. They also made a great image of the Great Bear and set it up in the center of the village. They offered gifts to the image and prayed to it, asking it not to harm them.

"Great Bear, we are afraid of you.
You are strong and we are weak.
You have killed and you have lived.
You have waited for two hundred years.
Now we are here and you are there.
Let us live in peace, Great Bear."
After that the young men went on hunting and fishing as before, and the voice of the Great Bear was never heard again.

The End

The story of "The Great Bear" is one of the most widely known among the Tlingit and Haida of the Northwest Coast. The story is told by many different tribes and in many different versions. The story is about the Great Bear, who was once a man but was killed and thrown in the water. Now he lives again as the Great Bear and waits for the time when he will rise up and kill all the little men. The story is told to explain why there are no bears in the area and why there is a high palisade around the village.

The young men saw a canoe approaching them and they called out to it, asking who was in the canoe.  The only reply was the sound of paddling.  Approaching very close, the young men could see that there was no one in the canoe, but that it was being propelled by a single arm.  The young men were mystified and disturbed by this and paddled hard to catch the canoe.  When they reached it, they were prepared to take the arm that was propelling it, but it disappeared into the fog.  They were then filled with sadness and cried out, "Poor spirit! We do not understand.  Go back to your people."  And the canoe gave a mournful cry and disappeared into the fog.

Later, the young men met an old chief and related to him what had happened.  The old chief explained that the arm was the arm of a spirit who had been in love with a young girl who lived long ago.  Her name was Tulip, and she was so beautiful that the sun hid its face whenever she walked in the meadow.  The spirit loved her, but she did not return his love, and so he killed himself.  He had been waiting long ago for her to come back to the meadow, but she never came.  The young men were told to leave him alone, for he was sad and should not be disturbed.

This story is from the Kwakwáká'waḱw (Kwakiutl) of the Pacific Northwest Coast.  It is found in the collections of the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland.

The story is set in the past, and the characters in the story are all native people. Context
The "Two Young Men of Egulac" is a common theme in native literature and folklore.  This particular version of the story is from the Kwakwaka'wakw people of the central coast of British Columbia.  The Kwakwaka'wakw are a native people who have a strong oral tradition, and many of their stories have been recorded and translated into written form by anthropologists and linguists.  This version of the story was recorded by John Marr in 1954, and it was translated from the native language by John Radford and Ronald Williams in 1966.  The story is a version of the "Two-in-One" theme, which is found in many cultures around the world.  The story can be interpreted as a coming of age story, in which the two young men are tested by the chief.  The story can also be interpreted as a story about the consequences of action and reaction.  The two young men's actions cause the chief to react, and the chief's reaction causes the young men to react.  The story can also be interpreted as a story about the relationship between humans and nature.  The two young men are out on the river hunting seals, which is a common activity for native people in this region, but their actions disrupt the natural order of things, and they are punished for their actions.

Analysis
This is a tale of the Kwakwaka'wakw, a native people of the west coast of Canada. It is a story of the supernatural, a genre common in the oral literature of many native peoples. In this tale, the young men are on a seal hunt and are frightened by the sound of voices calling in the fog. The third voice that explains the cause of the first two voices is that of the supernatural helper of the hunters. The tale is an example of the way that a native oral tradition can incorporate elements of European culture (in this case, the introduction of Christianity with the missionaries). The tale was recorded by Franz Boas, the famous anthropologist, in 1895.

The young men saw the fog as a spirit coming to take them with it to the land of the dead.  The young men began to sing and dance, and then the spirit took them and put them on a great journey.  It took them to the land of the dead, where they saw many things, and they heard the spirits of their ancestors singing.  Finally, the young men's bodies were returned to their families, but their spirits went on to the land of the dead, where they would live forever.

Context
The story of Egulac's young men is a creation myth from the Kwakiutl people of the Pacific Northwest.  It describes the journey of two young men who were taken by the spirit of the dead to the land of the dead.  This myth is linked to potlatching, the ceremonial redistribution of wealth, as the spirit of the dead man is said to return to the living world to hold a potlatch.  This myth is also linked to the Kwakiutl belief in the importance of ancestors, as the spirits of the dead are said to return and have a great influence on the living world.

Analysis
This myth can be analyzed in terms of the hero's journey.  The young men leave their home to go on a journey to the land of the dead.  They face death and are reborn, as their bodies are returned to their families but their spirits go on to the land of the dead.  This journey is a rite of passage, as the young men are reborn into the next stage of existence.  This myth can also be analyzed in terms of the concept of liminality, as the young men exist in a state between life and death, in the land of the dead.

Background
The story of the drowning of the two young men from Egulac is one of several traditional stories told by the Kwakwaka'wakw peoples of the west coast of Canada.  The story is told by Mungo Martin, a Kwakwaka'wakw artist and anthropologist, in his book "Mythology of the Kwakiutl Indians" (1957).  The story is one of several about the creation of the world and the people and creatures that inhabit it.  The story is also known as "The Drowning of the Two Young Men", "The Two Young Men Who Drowned", "The Egulac Boys", and "The Salmon Boy".

Analysis
In the story, the two young men are hunting seals when the water freezes over and they drown.  The story can be interpreted as a creation story, explaining the formation of the land and the bodies of water.  The story also has elements of a cautionary tale, warning of the dangers of the sea and the power of nature.
The story is also one of several that include a salmon boy.  In this story, the two young men are turned into salmon by the master of the undersea kingdom.  The master of the undersea kingdom appears in other stories as well, including "The Transformation of the Canoe".  In this story, a man is transformed into a canoe so that he may travel to the undersea kingdom and meet with the master of the undersea kingdom.  In "The Salmon Boy", the two young men are turned into salmon so that they may travel to the undersea kingdom and bring back a new potlatch box.

The young men from Egulac were afraid, so they lay flat in their canoe, not daring to breathe.  Then came a voice in the fog, "Do not be afraid.  We are from up the river. In another version of the tale, the young men from Egulac were out hunting seals when they were attacked by a group of Tlingit warriors in canoes.  The Egulac men fought back and killed all of their attackers.  When they returned to their village, they found that their enemies had been planning to attack them.  The Egulac men then decided to join forces with the Tlingit and become allies.

The story of "The Two Young Men from Egulac" is sometimes used by the Tlingit to explain why the two groups are friends instead of enemies.  The Tlingit and the people of Kake (formerly Egulac) are now united by law, culture, and friendship.  This story is also an example of the Tlingit's belief in spirits and the supernatural.

Kakwula told them to dry their skins and make themselves smart, then they would catch many seals. He told them to make a hole in the middle of their large communal skin and lie down inside it, with only their heads showing. Then, when the tide came in and the water touched their skin, it would be transformed into a great and powerful seal. The young men did as they were told, and soon a great seal came and touched their skin with its head. The young men then felt themselves lifted up and carried on the back of the great seal to a place where there were many other seals. The other seals did not dare to touch them, and the young men stayed with the seal all night, catching many other seals. In the morning, they returned to their own people, who were very surprised to see them return with so many seals. From then on, this method was used by the Kwakiutl to catch seals.

Analysis
This myth is a common type of transformation myth, involving a human being transformed into an animal or vice versa. The myth explains the origin of the Kwakiutl method of seal hunting, which was very important to their culture. The myth also contains elements of the trickster myth, as Kakwula is a trickster figure who uses cleverness to help the protagonists achieve their goal. The myth may also have a shamanistic element, as the young men are said to have "entered into the body of the seal".

Suddenly one of them cried out, "Behold! The whole universe is one being!" And they went on talking about the unity of all things, and when they returned to the village they found that the whole tribe was in the same state of mind, and so they decided that a great chief had died, and they built a big tower in memory of him.

Background
The story is one of a series of 8,000 tales, legends, and oral histories that were recorded by Francis James Boas in the late 19th century and early 20th century from Native American tribes in what is now British Columbia, Canada. The tribes that the stories came from include the Kwakiutl, Heiltsuk, Bella Coola, Bella Bella, Haida, Tlingit, and others. Most of the tribes that Boas recorded stories from spoke Wakashan languages, though some spoke Salish languages. The stories were collected from tribes along the coast of the North Pacific Ocean from the Northern California to the southern tip of the Alaska Peninsula.

Interpretation
The story of the two young men from Egulac is an example of what Boas called a "cosmos tale", which tells about the creation of the universe. The story also shows the influence of Christianity on Native American stories, as the idea that "the whole universe is one being" is a Christian concept. The story also shows the influence of the tribes' contact with Europeans and Americans from the Eastern United States, as the word "behold" is an English word and the tribes in British Columbia had little contact with Americans from the Eastern United States.

Background
The Empress of Japan was a Canadian Pacific Steamship that sank off the coast of British Columbia in 1919. The ship was en route from Vancouver to Victoria with a number of passengers and crew. The ship's manifest indicates that 27 passengers were on board, 15 of whom were crew members. The cause of the sinking was a collision with a rock.

The story
The Haida people believed that when a person died, they became a spirit and were joined by a totem animal, which would escort them to the land of spirits. The young men who had gone seal hunting saw the spirits of the people who had died on the Empress of Japan, followed by the totems of the Raven and the Thunderbird. The spirits told the young men that the Empress of Japan was a mighty ship, and that it had been under the control of the Thunderbird, which had flown down from the sky to test its strength against the great ship. The ship had been broken to pieces and the people on board had been taken to the land of spirits. The young men were told to return to their village and tell their people what they had seen.

Suddenly they heard a noise and one of them said: "It's only the wind". But a moment later they heard it again and the other man said: "It's only a seal". Then a third time they heard it and the first man said: "It's the Little People".

Background
The story of the "Little People" is a traditional tale told by the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. It has been collected and retold by ethnographers and anthropologists, and is included in the 1954 anthology Myths of the North American Indians, edited by Mischa Titiev.

Plot
The two young men from Egulac, a coastal village, went down to the river to hunt seals. After some time, they heard a noise and the first man said it was only the wind. But the noise came again, and the second man said it was only a seal. Then the noise came a third time, and the first man said it was the Little People. The second man laughed at this, and the first man explained that the Little People did not like it when people laughed at them, and that they could make trouble. Soon after, a great wave came ashore and drowned the two hunters.
The story has several variations. In one, the hunters are warned by a hermit to stay by the shore, but they do not listen to him, and are drowned by a wave. In another, the Little People are said to have given the hunters a warning, but they did not understand it, and were drowned.

Interpretation
The story likely arose from actual events, a shipwreck or drowning, and was later embellished with the supernatural elements. The Little People are not malevolent, but are annoyed by people who do not respect their domain, and punish them by causing a wave.

The source of this myth is from an oral tradition of the Tlingit people.

Analysis
This myth can be analyzed through the lens of Freudian psychoanalysis. According to Freud, the unconscious mind is made up of the id, ego, and superego.  The id is the most primitive part of the psyche and seeks pleasure and avoids pain. The ego serves as the mediator between the id and the external world. The superego is the moral part of the psyche that contains the individual's conscience.
In this myth, the id is represented by the two young men who go down to the river to hunt seals. The ego is represented by the young men who mediate between the young men's desire to have sex with the spirit woman and the consequences of their actions. The superego is represented by the spirit woman who is drowned for wading in the water.

Plot
A young man named Nootka lived with his father in a village on the northwest coast of America.  One day Nootka's father told him that he was going away for a month and that Nootka should not leave the village.  Nootka obeyed his father's command and stayed in the village.  One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm.  Nootka saw a canoe approaching them and called out to the occupant.  The occupant replied that it was only a dream.  Nootka was amazed that he could see so far in the fog.  The two young men returned to the village and told Nootka that they had seen a man in a canoe.  Nootka then realized that it was not a dream.  The next day Nootka's father returned and he was very angry that Nootka had disobeyed his command.  Nootka apologized and his father forgave him.  Nootka's father told him that he was going away for a long time and that Nootka should take care of the village.  Nootka did as he was told and one day he saw a man in a canoe approaching the village.  The man landed his canoe and Nootka went to speak to him.  The man told Nootka that he was a chief and that he had come to visit Nootka's village.  Nootka showed the chief the respect due to his rank and the chief was pleased.  The chief told Nootka that he would stay in the village for a month and then he would return to his own people.  Nootka was happy that he had obeyed his father's command to stay in the village.  After a month the chief returned to his own people and Nootka's father also returned.  Nootka told his father about the chief and his visit and his father was pleased that Nootka had obeyed his command.

Background
The story is one of many told by Fred Manning, an elder of the Tlingit people of the Yakutat area of Alaska. Manning was born in 1901 and grew up in the traditional Tlingit way, but when he was a young man he was sent to a mission school run by the Presbyterian Church. After leaving the school he went to Sitka, Alaska where he worked as a fisherman and logger. In 1942 he was taken to Fort Richardson near Anchorage where he worked in the mess hall. After the war he returned to Yakutat where he worked as a fisherman and logger until he retired. Manning died in 1980 at the age of 79.

The story of Uma is an example of a genre of Northwest Coast folklore known as "transformer tales", in which a human being changes into an animal or a bird, or vice versa. This particular tale is also an example of a genre of transformer tales in which the transformation is only temporary, and in which the transformed being lives for a time in the world of humans, before returning to the world of animals or birds. In this tale, the central character, Uma, is a seal-person, or um'olgoos.

The young men were frightened and called out to the spirits in the name of their grandfather, the great chief Kunwarch. Variants
This story is also known as "The Coming of the Twins."  It is told by the Nootka, Makah, and other coastal tribes of the North West Coast.  In some versions the spirits are not the twins, but the spirits of the hunters' ancestors who were killed by the white man.  In some versions the spirits do not ride back with the hunters, but go home with them at the end of the story.

Commentary
This story is about the reincarnation of the spirits of the dead.  The twins are the spirits of the hunters' ancestors, who died long ago.  The story tells how the spirits come back to life in the bodies of two young boys.  This is an example of how the belief in reincarnation can help a people deal with the loss of loved ones.  The story also shows how the Nootka people viewed the white men, as beings with red faces who killed their people with a disease.  The story also shows how the Nootka people hunted seals, an important food source for them.

Story
The two young men, Nootka and Calah, decided to explore the strange land.  They soon came upon a village, and saw people playing stick game.  The two young men joined in, and soon became very good at the game.  The people of the village were amazed at their skill, and called them "The Two Gods Come to Life".  Nootka and Calah were given the best food and every comfort.  But they missed their home and decided to return.
The village chief gave them a canoe and provisions, and they set out on their journey. When they arrived back in Egulac, they told their story to the people.  From then on, they were known as the "Two Heroes Who Traveled to the East".

The Great Treaty of the Salmon River (French: Le grand traité de la Rivière-à-l'Echelle) is a legend recounting an imaginary peace treaty between the Haudenosaunee and European settlers in Canada. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The legend is recounted in Jacques Cartier's journal, but it is generally considered to be a fabrication.

Jacques Cartier's journal
The legend is recounted in Jacques Cartier's journal, under the date of August 25, 1497. However, Cartier never even came close to the Salmon River (Rivière-à-l'Echelle) in 1497, and it is unlikely that he was even aware of its existence. The journal was not written by Cartier, but by Louis Penart, a member of the 1534 Champagne expedition, and it is generally considered to be a fabrication.
The legend is sometimes used to support the claim that Canada was discovered in the name of peace.

Variants
The legend is sometimes retold as if Cartier had visited the Gulf of St. Lawrence in 1497 (he did not), and had met an Iroquoian confederacy led by Hiawatha (who lived much later).

Suddenly they heard a sound and saw a light coming towards them. They thought it must be ghosts, but they were not afraid. They called out to the ghosts and asked where they came from and where they were going. The ghosts replied that they were Kwakities, who lived in the river, and that they were going to take the two young men with them. The young men were happy and went with them. The Kwakities gave them beautiful clothes to wear and put them on. Then the young men grew very large and heavy, and the Kwakities put them in a canoe and set them down on a sandbank. The two young men then went home, and no one believed their story.

Analysis
This is one of Boas' most famous Native American stories. It is a classic example of Boas' belief that the study of Native American folklore could only be truly understood by taking the Native American's point of view. The story is a good example of Boas' belief that Native American mythology was not a static entity, but was constantly changing. The story was recorded in 1895, and published in 1896. Boas believed that the story was a reinterpretation of a traditional Kwakiutl myth, that had been influenced by Christianity. The Kwakities are a Christianized version of the Kwakiutl tribe, and the story contains elements of the Christian story of Adam and Eve, along with elements of the traditional Kwakiutl mythology.

The young men heard voices coming from the water. At first they thought they were alone but soon they realized that the voices were coming from the spirits of the dead. The spirits informed the young men that they were going to die and that they should return to their village to prepare for their death.
The young men returned to their village and told the elders of their encounter with the spirits. The elders told them that this was a sign of their impending death and that they should make peace with their fellow villagers. The young men spent the next few days making peace with the other villagers and saying farewell to their loved ones. Soon after, the two young men were attacked and killed by a group of bandits.
After their death, the spirits of the young men came back to the river and joined the spirits of the dead. From then on, the villagers heard voices coming from the water on calm and foggy nights.

Cultural significance
The story of the Two Young Men of Egulac is a traditional Coast Salish story told by the Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. It is a common belief among Indigenous peoples that spirits of the dead can be encountered in the natural world, and that these spirits can provide warnings and messages to the living. The story also emphasizes the importance of making peace with others and preparing for one's death.

Suddenly they heard a noise and looked around, and saw a canoe approaching them. It was filled with ghosts!
The two young men were terrified and tried to paddle to the shore, but the ghosts in the canoe were quick, and soon they were surrounded. Then the leader of the ghosts spoke to them. He told them that they had been hunting seals too, long ago, and had been killed by the white man. They had been wandering around ever since, and had come across the two young men just now. The ghosts offered to let them go if they promised not to hunt seals anymore. The two young men agreed, and the ghosts rowed away, leaving them alone in the fog.

Background
This story is one of many told by Ursula K. Le Guin in her 1978 collection "Dancing at the Edge of the World". The stories are about a fictional island in the Pacific Ocean called "Ekumma" (or "Egulac") and its people. Le Guin's mother was an anthropologist who did fieldwork among the Ila people of the Pacific Northwest Coast, and the stories are influenced by the anthropological and linguistic knowledge she passed on to Le Guin. The stories are told from the point of view of an ethnographer who is interviewing the narrator, and they include the narrator's comments on the ethnographer's questions and observations.
The story is an example of Le Guin's exploration of the idea that the boundary between the real and the imaginary is permeable. In this story, she uses the idea of ghosts to explore the consequences of hunting seals, which were (and still are) hunted to the point of endangerment.

Plot
A long time ago, in a village along the Fraser River, two young men go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, a fog comes in and it becomes calm. The hunters hear a sound and one of them says it is an otter. The other man says no, it is the wind. A voice comes from the water and it is an otter. The woman whose voice it is tells the hunters that her husband killed her child, a girl, and that he had drowned himself and her together.

Variants
The story has a variant in which a woman drowns herself and her two children because her husband has left her.

Discussion
The story is one of a class of Northwest Coast Indian stories that are called "transformers" because they tell how the world as we know it came into being. In this story, the world as we know it is one in which people live in villages along the river and hunt seals. The story also tells how the Northwest Coast came to be populated by people who are now alive.
The story also contains a moral about the importance of knowing things for sure before you speak.

Origin
The story is from the Kwakiutl, a Native American culture that is part of the Northwest Coast culture area.

Variants
The story has been recorded in several variants, including one in which a woman drowns herself and her two children because her husband has left her.

They heard a strange sound over the water, and they headed for the shore. When they reached the bank they saw a young woman sitting in a canoe.  They asked her who she was and where she came from, and she replied that she was the spirit of the river.  She warned them that they would die if they went any further, and then she vanished. Analysis
This is a classic example of a type of story known as a "scenes-from-a-life," in which a series of short, seemingly unconnected episodes represent the entire life of a character.  The story is rich in sensory detail, and the narrator takes pains to emphasize the beauty and power of the natural world.  The presence of the spirit of the river is an example of the belief in "guardian spirits" that is found in many Native American cultures.

The young men saw a canoe approaching and heard someone call out to them. It was their friend Kokos, who had been hunting seals also. Kokos told them that he had killed five seals, and invited them to share in the meat. They accepted, and as they were eating, Kokos began to sing. As he sang, the two young men became very sorrowful, and Kokos asked them why they were weeping. They replied that they were weeping because of the loss of their people, who had died of disease. Kokos sang a second time, and again the young men wept. This time, Kokos explained that he was singing of the time when the world was new, and all the people were happy. The young men realized that they had been crying for the loss of their past happiness, and felt better. Kokos took them home, and as they landed at their village, Kokos's canoe was swallowed up by the earth.

Variants
This story is also known as "The Song of the Seal Hunter," and has been recorded among the Nootka, Makah, and Hupa. In some versions, the hero's name is given as Kokopelli, and in others he is a woman. In some versions, the hunters are not from Egulac, and the woman who weeps is Kokopelli's wife.

Interpretation
The story can be interpreted as a lament for the loss of the old ways of life, and the change to a more modern way of living. The seal hunting represents the old ways, and the swallowing up of Kokopelli's canoe represents the loss of the old culture. The story also has elements of the trickster figure, as Kokopelli is able to change the mood of the story from sadness to happiness. The story also has elements of creation myth, as Kokopelli's singing creates a new world for the listeners.

Suddenly one of them cried out "Behold! A thousand horns!" and he flung up his arm and pierced the fog with a loud and terrible scream. Then the other one cried out "Behold! A thousand eyes!" and he too threw up his arm and joined the first one in the terrible scream.

Context
This passage comes from a chapter in Mildred Armstrong Kalish's book titled "The Inland Sea".  In this chapter, Kalish describes a canoe trip she took with her husband Frank along the Inside Passage of the west coast of Canada from Vancouver Island to the Queen Charlotte Islands.  The story was told to her by a Tlingit woman named Mary Lee Dauenhauer while they were visiting Kake, Alaska.

Analysis
The story is a good example of the genre of Northwest Coast Indian folklore known as "encounter myths", in which a Native person encounters a being or beings from the supernatural world.  In this story, the two young men are out hunting and accidentally summon two supernatural beings.  The response of the men is to scream in terror and throw up their arms.  The beings are described as having "a thousand horns" and "a thousand eyes", which suggests that they are monstrous beings.
This story also contains elements of the Tlingit creation story, in which Raven the Trickster is responsible for bringing light to the world.  In this story, the young men's screams are like the scream that Raven let out when he brought light to the world.

Background
The story of the White Pine is one of many told by Canadian author Maude Louise Percy in her 1916 collection of folklore, The Ojibway Man. The Ojibway are an Anishinaabe people whose traditional territory covers much of northern Canada and the United States. This story is an example of a kind of tale known as a "revenge tale", in which a wronged spirit seeks vengeance.

Analysis
The White Pine story is an example of the way in which traditional Indigenous stories can reflect the effects of colonization and cultural contact. In this story, the White Pine's desire for revenge against the lumber men represents the frustration and anger that many Indigenous peoples feel in the face of colonization and the destruction of their lands and cultures. This story can also be read as a commentary on the way in which the natural world can be viewed as possessing agency and the ability to seek revenge.

Plot
The story begins by describing the beauty of the landscape, and two young men from the village of Egulac going down to the river to hunt seals.  They are successful in their hunt and while they are there it becomes foggy and calm.  The narrator then describes the appearance of a canoe and a voice calling out, "Do not shoot! This is a trap."  The young men are startled but continue with their work.  Suddenly they hear laughter and see that the moon has turned red.  They realize that spirits are present and one of the young men falls ill.  He is taken to the village shaman who tells him that he has been marked by the spirits.  The young man asks to be taken back to the place where he was marked so that he can make offerings to the spirits.  The shaman and his assistant go with him and they are met by a group of spirits led by the spirit of the chief.  The young man is offered a pipe and smokes with the spirits.  The chief tells him that he has been chosen to be a medicine man and will be given the power to heal.  The young man returns to the village and tells his people of his experience.  From that day on, he is a powerful healer.

Context
The story is one of several that are part of the larger Sisiutl legend cycle that is shared by the communities along the northwest coast of North America.  The Sisiutl story cycle is a complex and layered narrative about the origins of the world and the people living in it.  The story of the Red Moon is a healing narrative that explains how one individual becomes a healer.  The story is also an example of the way that oral narratives can change and develop over time.  While the basic story remains the same, the details can change depending on the teller and the audience.  The story of the Red Moon has been told by members of the Kwakwaka'wakw communities on the northwest coast of British Columbia, Canada.

He asked her to marry him, but she said she could not because she was in love with the other young man who was with him. The two young men then decided to have a duel to determine who would be able to marry her. They used their seal-hunting spears as weapons. The man who was in love with the woman he asked out was a better spear-thrower, and he killed his rival. The woman was so upset that her beloved was killed that she jumped into the water and drowned herself.

The young man who died left behind a little boy, named Kwa'sak'sak. He grew up to become a great warrior and leader. The young man who survived married the other woman, and they had a little girl. The two young women later died of grief.

Years later, Kwa'sak'sak and his wife went to a potlatch given by the man who had killed his father. Kwa'sak'sak's wife was given a blanket as a gift, which was the same blanket that had been given to her mother long ago. Kwa'sak'sak realized that the blanket had passed through three generations of women, and he knew that the woman who had sung so beautifully was the cause of his father's death and his own misery. He became so angry that he killed the potlatch chief.

Kwa'sak'sak then fled to the mountains and lived there alone. After some time, he decided that he would return to his people and live in peace. But when he got to the village, he was told that it was no longer safe to live there. The village was threatened by a great flood, and no one knew how to stop it. Kwa'sak'sak decided that he would go up to the mountains to ask the Great Chief for help. The Great Chief told him that the only way to stop the flood was to kill the sea-god. Kwa'sak'sak did this, and the flood stopped. Kwa'sak'sak then returned to his people and lived with his wife in peace.

The young men saw a canoe approaching them and they called out: "Who is there?" The canoe came close enough to see that it was only the reflection of the sky on the water.

Plot
The story is set in the Pacific Northwest of Canada, in a place called Egulac. Two young men, Loo-wass-a-quick and Loo-wass-a-little, go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, it becomes foggy and calm. The young men see a canoe approaching them. They call out, "Who is there?" The canoe comes close enough for them to see that it is only the reflection of the sky on the water. Suddenly, a seal jumps up and the young men shoot it. They have only one bullet left, so they decide to shoot at the next seal that jumps up. However, instead of a seal, a woman appears. She is the spirit of the land. The young men are amazed and ask her why she appears as a woman. The woman says that she always appears as what the person wants to see. The young men ask her for a gift and the woman gives them a potlatch. When the young men return to their village, they give a potlatch and are respected by all. The story ends with the narrator saying that this is the tale of two young men who became great chiefs.

Analysis
This story is a good example of the supernatural events that can be found in many Northwest Coast Native stories. The story also shows the respect that the Natives had for the land and the spirits that inhabited it. It also shows the generosity of the spirits, who give the young men a potlatch, which in turn raises their social status. The story also shows the Native belief in reincarnation, as the young men become chiefs. The story also shows the importance of the potlatch ceremony.

Variants
There are no variants of this story.

Plot
One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. While they were there, it became foggy and calm. The young men saw a canoe approaching and heard someone call out to them. It was their friend Onatsi, who told them to be careful because the seal hunt was forbidden to them. The young men were captured by a group of supernatural beings who lived in the sea and were taken to a strange land where they were forced to work as slaves. They were given the task of filling a large basket with sand, but no matter how much they filled it, it was never full. Their task was to keep filling it until they died. The young men worked for many years, but Onatsi managed to escape and returned to Egulac to warn the people.

Variants
This story has been collected under many different names, but is best known as "The Legend of the Sea-People". It has been collected from a number of Native American groups, including the Kwakiutl, Heiltsuk, Nootka, Tlingit, and Haida.

Interpretation
"The Legend of the Sea-People" is a trickster tale, with Onatsi playing the role of the trickster. The story describes the consequences of violating a taboo. In this case, the young men from Egulac violated the taboo against hunting seals, which resulted in their capture and enslavement by the sea-people. The story also describes a journey to the land of the dead.

So the young men returned to their boat and the god asked them why they were afraid.  They replied that it was because they had heard that he was a terrible god. The myth of the seal god Olaluk appears to be related to the much older mythology of the Thunderbird and the Sea-Monster from the eastern woodlands. Plot
The narrator begins by stating that only those who have heard the waters speak can understand the story. One night two young hunters from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. They heard the waters speak to them, and the older man suggested that they return to their canoe and go home, but the younger man was fascinated by the waters' voices and wanted to stay. The older man finally consented, but as they were returning to their canoe, the younger man stopped and ran back to the river. The older man waited for him, but he did not return, and after waiting for a long time, he went back to the place where they had heard the waters speak and sat down. He was later found dead.

The story of the "sea monster" is a common one in the folklore of many cultures.  In this particular version, the two young men are out hunting on the coast when they encounter the monster. In all of these variants, the hero or heroes must use all of their wits and courage to escape from the monster and return home safely.

The story of the seal people
Once upon a time, in a far away land, there was a tribe of people who lived by the sea.  They were called the Egulac people.  The Egulac people were hunters and fishermen.  They lived in harmony with the creatures of the sea.  One day two young men from the Egulac tribe went down to the river to hunt seals.  It was a foggy and calm night.  As they were there, a great many seals swam upstream.  The two men realized that the noise they heard was made by the seals they had disturbed, and that the sound traveled downstream ahead of them.  They saw that the seals were trying to protect their young, which were left behind in the caves while the adults went out to feed.  The two men were filled with awe and respect for the seals and their social structure.  From that day on, the Egulac people respected the seal people and their way of life, and they never hunted seal pups again.  The story of the seal people was passed down through the generations, and the Egulac people continued to live in harmony with the creatures of the sea.

The young men saw the fog come in closer and closer to the shore, and eventually they saw a canoe approaching them. In the canoe were four young men from Kowloon, who had also gone out to hunt seals. The two young men from Egulac invited their Kowloon counterparts to share their meal, and also offered to share the seal meat with them when they had finished hunting. The Kowloon men accepted both offers, and the four sat down together to share the meal.
As they ate, the young men from Egulac began to talk about their experiences. They spoke of the many things they had seen in their travels, and told of their experiences at Fort Vancouver. They spoke of the many different peoples they had met there, and of the "black robed priests" they had seen there, who carried crosses. They spoke of the large black ship that had come to the fort last summer, and of the many other ships that were usually there. They spoke of the great American flag that flew over the fort, and of the British flag that was also often seen there.
The Kowloon men listened carefully to all of these words, and asked questions about some of the things they did not understand. The young men from Egulac answered all their questions, and told them all they could about the white people and their fort. When they had finished eating, the Kowloon men thanked their hosts, and invited them to come and visit them in their village sometime. The young men from Egulac accepted the invitation, and the Kowloon men then pushed off and returned to their own people.

Suddenly they heard a noise and looked around, and saw a canoe approaching.  In it was a young woman.  She was all alone.  The young men were astonished and asked her where she came from, and she answered that she was from Hoy, where she lived with her parents.  She asked them where they lived, and they told her they were from Egulac, where they lived with their parents.  She asked them what they were doing there, and they told her they were hunting seals.  She told them that she was also hunting seals, and asked if she could go with them, and they told her she could.  So she went with them.  And that is how, according to the story, the people of Hoy came to be.

Background
The Kwakiutl, like many indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest, had a complex system of exogamous matrilineal clans.  Each clan had its own crest, and was associated with a particular territory.  The people of Hoy, who traced their descent through their mothers, were the crest-keepers for the sea-otter.  The story of the discovery of Hoy is one of several origin stories that explain the presence of the people of different villages and tribes in the region.

Variants
The story is known in slightly different versions under the names "How Hoy Was Discovered" and "The Discovery of Hoy".  There are several variants of the story of the discovery of Hoy, collected from different informants.  In one version, the two young men are out hunting seals when they hear a noise and see a woman in a canoe.  They ask her who she is, and she replies that she is the daughter of the chief of Hoy.  She asks them who they are, and they tell her that they are from Egulac.  She tells them that she is also out hunting seals, and asks if she can go with them.  They agree, and she goes with them.  When they return to their village, they tell the other people about the beautiful woman they met.  The other young men are jealous, and decide to go and meet her.  But when they get to Hoy, they find that she has promised to marry one of the young men who discovered Hoy.

Talequa said to the strangers, "I am chief of this river. What do you want?"

Talequa felt sorry for the strangers, but he knew that he could not let them take over their land. He said, "There is a place where you can live. It is a long way from here. Go there and stay there. Do not come back here."
The strangers left and went to the place where Talequa had told them to go. They found it to be a very good place. They lived there and became strong and prosperous.
The Yaquina people were glad that they had met the strangers because they had given them a new home. From then on the Yaquina and the people from the north lived together as one people.

Legend
Once upon a time, long ago, two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. It was winter, and the river was frozen over. While they were there, it became foggy and calm. Suddenly, they saw in the distance the double-headed sea serpent. One head of the serpent faced upstream, and the other head faced downstream.
The young men were very afraid, but they did not dare to run away. They were afraid that the serpent would see them run away and chase them. They knew that if the serpent chased them, it would kill them.
The young men knew that the only way to save themselves was to remain perfectly still and not make a sound. The serpent swam around them for a long time, but it did not see them. Finally, it swam away and was gone.
The young men went back to their village and told the other people about the serpent. The other people did not believe them, and they laughed at the young men. But the young men knew that what they had seen was real. From then on, the young men never went down to the river to hunt seals again.

Variations
In another version of the legend, the young men are out hunting seals on the sea ice when the sea serpent appears. The serpent is so large that it blocks out the sky. The young men crouch down behind their sled runners, and the serpent passes right by them.

Inspiration
The legend of the double-headed sea serpent is one of many legends about sea serpents told by the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. The story may have been inspired by sightings of large sea animals, such as a pair of sea lions or a large school of fish, or by the imagination of the storyteller.

Context

Analysis
The story shows the importance of music and nature to the culture of the Blackfoot people. The two young men and women sing together, and it is said that they sang until the sky was light again. This shows that music is a very powerful and important thing to the culture. Also, the fact that the young men and women join the two main characters shows that it is a communal activity. This is also shown when the two young men go out together to hunt seals. It is a group activity that brings the community together. Another important aspect of the story is the fact that it takes place at night, and that the characters are hunting seals. Seals are an important food source for the Blackfoot people, and hunting them shows the practicality of the culture.

Plot
The story begins by describing a flat-bottomed boat with two young men from the Haida village of Egulac. They are hunting seals near the mouth of the Taku River. It is a foggy and calm night. Suddenly they hear a great rumbling noise and see a huge sea-monster rising out of the water. They take a long time shooting it and finally kill it. When they examine the monster, they find that it is not a sea-monster but the bottom of a coal-ship that has run aground and been broken up by the waves. The narrator adds that the two young men were very disappointed.

Background
The story is a variant of the oral Haida folklore that is found in many Native American cultures. The Taku River is on the north coast of British Columbia, Canada. Coal ships do occasionally run aground on the sand bars at the mouth of the river.

Analysis
The story is a good example of the juxtaposition of two very different worlds found in the works of Bromley. In this case, the two worlds are that of the Haida Indians and the white men who are hunting seals. The two worlds are described in terms of their knowledge of the world around them. The Haida are intimately familiar with the sea and its creatures. They are able to hunt seals at night in a foggy and calm sea. Their knowledge is demonstrated by the length of time it takes them to kill the sea-monster. In contrast, the white men are from a world of coal-ships and technology. Their knowledge is demonstrated by the fact that they have a coal-ship that is large enough to run aground on the sand bars at the mouth of the Taku River. The two worlds are also described in terms of their reaction to the sea-monster. The Haida are disappointed when they find that the sea-monster is not real, while the narrator finds their disappointment amusing.

Plot
Set in the Pacific Northwest in the early 20th century, One Night Stand is a story of two young men from the indigenous Egulac tribe who go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, it becomes foggy and calm. One of them says to the other that he thinks he hears someone singing, but when they listen closely, they hear nothing. Suddenly, an old man appears and says that he hears their thoughts.
The young men are astonished and ask the old man how he came there. He replies that he had been living in the river for many years. The young men then ask him to teach them how to sing the songs that he has heard in the river. The old man agrees, but he warns them that the songs are very powerful, and that they must be careful how they use them.
The young men learn the songs from the old man, and as they sing them, they begin to understand the power that the old man warned them about. They sing the songs to the seals, and the seals come right up to their boat. The young men then begin to understand the power of the songs, and the power of their connection to the land and the water.

Production
One Night Stand was produced in 1983 by the National Film Board of Canada. The film was written and directed by Brian J. Smith, and produced by Geraldine Wagner. The film was shot on location in the Broughton Archipelago, on the northwest coast of Canada.

Reception
One Night Stand won the Best Short Film Award at the 1984 Canadian Film Awards. The film was also screened at the 1984 Festival of Festivals, later known as the Toronto International Film Festival, where it was named one of five "Discoveries" by the Festival Programmers.

Plot
Shalala fell in love with one of the young men, and gave herself to him. The young man was disappointed in his lover's infidelity, but decided to return with his friend to their village. They heard a strange noise and one said to the other: "I wonder what that is." "It's probably only a log," the other replied. "But if it's only a log, why does it make that noise?" "You're always asking so many questions," the other man said. "Why don't you just shoot it?"

Plot
The story is set in the Pacific Northwest of North America. The narrator describes a friendship between two young men of the Egulac tribe. The friends go to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, a strange noise is heard. One man thinks it may be a log, but why would a log make that noise? He wonders. His friend tells him to shoot it if he thinks it is bothering them. The friend's response makes the man realize that his friend is not like him, that his friend is satisfied with just living and not always questioning things. The man then realizes that he is different from his friend and that he must leave.

Analysis
The story is an example of the "Northwest Coast" style of short story. The story is more about atmosphere and mood than about a clear and logical sequence of events. The story's meaning is not clearly stated, but it can be inferred that the author is saying that there are many ways to look at the world and that all are valid. The story can also be seen as a commentary on the influence of European culture on Native American culture. The European style of clear thinking and logic is in contrast to the Native American style of accepting the world as it is.

Title
The title of the story refers to the idea that reality is not as it seems.

Suddenly they heard a great rushing sound, and as they looked up they saw a huge wave coming towards them. They tried to run up the bank, but the wave was too fast, and they were caught by it and drawn out into the water. Just as they gave up hope of living, they were plunged into deep water and held there for a few moments. Then they were lifted up again, and felt the wave carrying them on to the shore. They ran inland and lay down to rest, and as they lay there, they felt all over their bodies as if they were being stung by insects. They got up and ran to a tree for protection, and as they leaned against it, they felt the same stinging all over their backs. They looked at each other in surprise, and then they saw that their backs were covered with foam, and that the tree was covered with beads of sweat.

The young men then realized that the wave was really the spirit of the river, and that the stinging was caused by the beads of sweat on the leaves of the tree. They were greatly afraid, and ran away and told the people in the village what had happened to them. The old men then told them that this was the way the spirits of things showed themselves to young men who were about to become great hunters or warriors. After this the two young men grew up to be great hunters and warriors, and killed many enemies and brought home many victories to their people.

The old men also told them that, long ago, the river had been a man who was very kind to everyone, but who was sad because he had no children. One day he went down to the seashore to hunt seals, and while he was there he changed into a wave and went out to meet a great enemy wave that was coming towards him. The two waves met and held each other, and then the enemy wave went back to the east, and the man wave went back to the village, and from that time on the people saw the river as a great wave whenever it was angry.

Context
The story is found in the oral traditions of the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) people on the west coast of Vancouver Island, in what is now Canada. It is related by Roy Henry Vickers, a Tla-o-qui-aht artist and author, in his 1981 book Northwest Coast Indian Mythology.

Analysis
According to anthropologist and author George S. Hendricks, the story is an example of a shaman's journey in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology. He states that the story contains several typical elements, including the journey to the land of the dead, a feast with the spirits, and a message from the spirits for the people.Hendricks notes that the story also contains an element of social commentary, as it implies that the Nuu-chah-nulth had been forcibly removed from their land by European settlers. He writes that this is likely a reference to the 1896 opening of the Nootka Sound fishery, which brought many white fishermen to the area and led to conflicts with the Nuu-chah-nulth.

Analysis
This is a classic example of a legend explaining a natural phenomenon.  The Chinook people lived on the shores of the Columbia River and the Pacific Ocean, and were well aware that the tides and currents could be dangerous.  This legend explains why, in certain conditions, a person might be seized by the water and carried away.

Variants
This legend is known by many different names, including The Spirit of the Water, The Woman in the Water, and The White Lady of the Columbia.  It is also told by several different Native American tribes along the Pacific Northwest coast, including the Chinook, the Clatsop, and the Tillamook.  The Clatsop version is told from the point of view of a woman who was out seal hunting with her husband.  In this version, the monster who seizes the husband is identified as "the spirit of a great chief who had been killed long ago".  The Tillamook version adds a detail in which the monster carries the man away to a cave under the sea, where he is transformed into a seal and lives for 100 years before being transformed back into a man.

Suddenly there was a great deal of noise and rushing water and when the fog lifted the young men saw that the Great Bear was catching salmon.
The Great Bear, also known as the Sea Otter Bear or White Bear, is a mythological creature said to be a giant bear that catches salmon in the waters along the coast of British Columbia. The story of the Two Young Men and the Great Bear is one of many variations of a common theme found in the oral literature of the Coast Salish peoples of the Pacific Northwest.

Variants
There are several variants of this story, some of which involve a man and a woman instead of two men. In some versions, the protagonists are tricked by the Great Bear rather than being allowed to watch him catch fish. In one version, a man and a woman are turned into stone by the Great Bear when they break one of his rules. In another version, a man who is turned into a bear by the Great Bear is later turned back into a man by the Great Raven.

Trickster versions
There are several trickster versions of this story. In one version, the Great Bear is tricked by Raven into revealing the location of his salmon fishing grounds. Once Raven knows where to find the salmon, he goes there and catches all the fish for himself. Another version has Coyote as the protagonist. In this version, Coyote tricks the Great Bear into revealing the location of his salmon fishing grounds, and then Coyote and his family live off the salmon for the rest of their lives.

Background
The story is from the Kwakiutl people of the Northwest Coast of North America. The Kwakiutl are a tribe of the indigenous peoples of Canada. The story is a creation myth which explains how the world was made. The people of the tribe believed that everything in the world had a dual nature and that everything had a counterpart in the sky.

Analysis
This myth has a number of similarities with other creation myths from around the world. The idea that the world was created from water is found in many cultures. In Genesis the world is created from water. In Hindu mythology the god Vishnu is said to have created the world from water. In the Mayan creation myth the first gods were born from the sea. The idea that the world was created from a series of transformations is also found in many myths. For example, in the Norse creation myth, the world is created from the body of a giant, Ymir.

Suddenly they heard a loud noise and looked around and saw a canoe capsize and all the Indians in it drown.

Plot
The narrator is an elderly Native American who recalls a story his grandfather used to tell him about two young men from the Egulac tribe who went down to the river to hunt seals. The narrator explains that his grandfather used to tell this story to keep the young men from going out in the canoes at night during the foggy seasons.
The two young men had gone out to hunt seals and while they were there, it became foggy and calm. Suddenly, they heard a loud noise and looked around and saw a canoe capsize and all the Indians in it drown. The narrator explains that the noise was caused by the wind blowing through the tall grasses that lined the riverbanks.
The narrator then describes how his grandfather used to tell the story differently, saying that the two young men were out hunting ducks when they were attacked by a giant sea monster. The narrator explains that his grandfather would change the story to make it more interesting for the young listeners.

Themes
The story explores the idea that history and memory are not always fixed or objective, but can be subjective and change over time. It also explores the idea of storytelling as a means of passing down culture and knowledge from one generation to the next.

Critical reception
The Canoe was praised by critics for its exploration of storytelling and memory. The Globe and Mail said of the story, "The Canoe is a lovely, haunting tale that explores the idea of memory and the way stories change and take on new meaning as they are passed down through the generations."

The two men heard voices in the fog calling out their names, and then they heard someone playing the violin. They followed the sound and came upon a beach where they saw thousands of people, all dressed in white, playing different musical instruments. The two men joined in, and played their own compositions on their instruments, a trumpet and a drum. When the music finished and the people disappeared, the two men returned to their canoe and continued their seal hunting, but they saw no more supernatural events that night.

Variants
This story is also known as The Music Makers, The Seal Hunters, and The People in the Mist.

Analysis
This story is a classic example of a vision quest narrative. The two young men go out into nature to have a vision, and are rewarded with a vision of a great community of people who are all connected to music and the natural world. The musical element is a common one in indigenous stories, and can be seen as a way of connecting the natural world to the spiritual world.

The young men saw a canoe approaching them and they called out to the occupants and asked who was there. It was their friends from upriver, who had heard the reports of the good hunting and came down to join them. The young men invited them to join in the hunt, and together they had a very successful hunt.
The next morning, however, the young men from downriver decided to leave and return upriver to their own village. The young men from Egulac were disappointed that their friends left so early, and they had not spoken to each other since.
Later, the young men from Egulac decided to visit their friends upriver, and they went to their village and were welcomed. The young men asked their friends why they did not stay the previous year, and their friends replied that they had heard there was a smallpox epidemic in Egulac and they did not want to risk getting sick and dying. The young men from Egulac were surprised by this news, as they had not heard there was smallpox in their village. Their friends told them that they had seen a group of people from Egulac come down the river with smallpox, and they had hidden in the bushes until the sick people passed. The young men from Egulac then realized that their visit had saved their friends' lives.

Background
The story is set in the context of the fur trade along the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America. The Nootka Sound region was a major centre for the fur trade in the 18th and early 19th centuries. The story relates a specific incident of intertribal friendship and cooperation in the context of the fur trade.

Variants
The story has been recorded in several variants, and in each variant the names of the tribes and locations change. For example, in one variant the tribes involved are the Tlingit and Haida, and the story takes place in the context of the salmon trade rather than the fur trade.

Suddenly they heard a loud noise and a huge shadow passed over them. Looking up, they saw that it was the Great Bear coming out of the water. The two young men were frightened and took off their clothes and swam to the opposite shore. When they got there, they picked up their clothes and saw that they were covered with blue spots. The two young men died when the Great Bear found and killed them.

Story origin
This story is a common one among the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian peoples of the Pacific Northwest. It is also found among the Chinook peoples of the Columbia River.

Story analysis
This story is a type of "marked man" tale, a common motif in world folklore. In this case, the young men have been marked for death by the Great Bear. The story may also reflect a belief in the transformative power of the bear, which can turn humans into bears or give them bear powers.

Story commentary
The story of the Two Boys Marked by the Bear is a tale of the power and mystery of nature. The young men are out on the river, hunting seals, when suddenly the power of nature is revealed to them in the form of the Great Bear. They are insignificant in the face of this power, and they know that they are doomed.

Story usage
This story can be used to illustrate the power of nature, the idea of the "marked man," and the belief in transformation. It can also be used to discuss the idea of fate, and the inevitability of death.

Teacher's guide
