The two young men were afraid, for fear of the water, and lay down behind a large log and did not dare move. Then suddenly, in the quiet and stillness, they heard the waters sing to them. This was the first time they had ever heard the waters speak. The young men were so frightened that they ran away and hid in the bushes. After that, they never told anyone of this experience, because they were too scared.

The older people of the tribe did not believe that the waters could speak, and told the young men that they had probably heard the wind in the reeds. The young men did not say anything, but they knew that it was the waters that had spoken to them.
One day, as the young men were out hunting, the chief's son fell into a freezing river and was drowned. The young men who had heard the waters speak came to rescue him, but it was too late. When the older men went to retrieve the body, they found the chief's son lying at the bottom of the river. The young men who had heard the waters speak were blamed for not trying hard enough to save the chief's son, and they were made to do all the work after that.
Later, the young men who had heard the waters speak were out hunting again, when a young woman from a neighbouring tribe came running up to them. She told them that their tribe was going to be attacked by warriors from the neighbouring tribe, and that she was the only one who had escaped. The young men knew that they could not protect the woman, or their own tribe, so they decided to leave.
They went to the place where they had first heard the waters speak, and asked the waters for help. The waters told them to go to the forest where the red cedar trees grew, and to cut down a tree and carve a message into the trunk. The young men did as the waters had said, and when they returned to their village, they found that it was empty. All their people had left, and the village was in ruins.
The young men went to the forest, and carved a message into a red cedar tree, and then they heard the waters speaking to them once again. The waters told them that their tribe had been moved to a new location, and that the young men should go to the new village and live there.

The young men saw a strange canoe heading towards them and they called out and asked who was in the canoe.  They received no answer, and as the canoe came closer they saw that it was headed by a human head which was on a stick and which kept turning around.  The young men were frightened and rowed back to the shore.  The canoe was headed by the spirit of a chief who was known to be very angry.  The young men had seen a spirit and had escaped with their lives.

Analysis
This story is an example of a genre of tales that are told in the coastal areas of British Columbia, in which the natural world is imbued with spirit power and human beings must take care not to offend the spirits of the land, the water, and the animals.  The story also reveals the importance of the Tlingit clan system and the respect that must be shown to the chiefs of the clans.  The tale can be read as an allegory in which the young men represent the living and the chief represents the dead.  The tale can also be read as a commentary on the power of fear and how it can be used to control others.

Variants
There are several variants of this tale, some of which are told by the Tsimshian people and the Haida people.  In the Tsimshian version, the young men are out seal hunting when they see a headless corpse in a canoe.  The corpse is that of a chief who was killed by the tribe.  The young men flee in terror and the chief returns to his people in the land of the dead.  In another variant, the young men are out fishing when they see a headless corpse in a canoe.  The corpse is that of a chief who was killed by the tribe.  The young men are so frightened that they throw down their fishing gear and flee.  The chief is pleased with their fear and decides not to take revenge.

They are not sure whether they should give in to the spirits' call, and paddle towards the spirit world, or whether they should resist and paddle away. Synopsis
One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. While they were there it became foggy and calm. The young men saw the sea serpent.
Subsequently, the young men told their tale to the other villagers, who decided to make a special excursion to see the serpent for themselves. The serpent was seen as a powerful being, and a good omen. However, after a short time, the serpent was seen as a threat, and the white man came to kill it.

Production
The film was shot in the summer of 1958 on the shores of Knight Inlet, on the west coast of Canada. The film was a joint production between the National Film Board of Canada and the University of British Columbia. The film's director, Cliff Hanley, was a contract director with the National Film Board of Canada.

Reception
The film was shown at the 1958 Festival of Festivals, where it was described as "a fascinating documentary of the Indian's life on the coast, and the interplay between the white man's civilisation and the ancient Indian customs."The film was reissued in 1976 as part of the National Film Board of Canada's Anthology series.

The story is told by an old Kwakiutl man to a white man, who does not understand the meaning of the part about the spirits.  The old man explains that the Kwakiutl believe that the souls of dead warriors enter into the bodies of their children, and that the children then become great warriors.  He also explains that the Kwakiutl used to be very warlike, but that now they only pretend to be, for the white men do not understand their real beliefs, and would kill them if they knew that the Kwakiutl did not really fight each other.

Overview
One Night is a 1998 Canadian short film directed by Kathleen Jayme. The film is based on a Haida legend and tells the story of two young men who venture out to hunt seals, only to encounter the sea god and his wife.The short film was produced by the National Film Board of Canada.

Synopsis
A long time ago, in a coastal village in the Great Bear Rainforest, two young men went out at night to hunt seals. While they were there, the calm and foggy conditions made the sea god angry. He and his wife rose up from the water, and the young men tried to hide. The sea god asked them why they were hiding, and the younger man replied that he was afraid of the sea god. The sea god then asked the younger man if he knew how big the world is, and if he knew that humans are just a tiny part of the world. The sea god then told the young men that they could go home, and that he would give them a gift: the ability to hunt seals at any time of the year.

The short film has no spoken dialogue, and the actors only make grunting and shouting noises.

Production
The film was shot on location in Masset, British Columbia, using local Haida actors and dancers. The film was co-produced by the National Film Board of Canada and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Suddenly, from the water came a long, low, and mournful sound like the wailing of human voices. The young men were afraid, and they ran away. They did not dare to look behind them or they might see the ghosts of those who had died long ago in the olden time.
The young men ran to the top of the bluff and looked down at the river. They saw a number of canoes coming towards them. The young men were afraid that the ghosts were following them. They were glad when the canoes passed below them and disappeared in the fog.
The young men returned to the village and told the people about the ghosts that they had seen. The old people said, "We have told you before that the Egulac people must not go down to the river to hunt seals. The river belongs to the ghosts, and they do not like to see anyone disturb their peace."

The people of Egulac were afraid to go down to the river, even to drink the water, for fear that the ghosts would be angry with them. They went to the old medicine man for advice. He told them to make an offering of tobacco and incense to the ghosts.
The people of Egulac did as the medicine man advised, and after that they were no longer afraid to go down to the river to hunt seals. The seals came up to the shore to be speared, and the people of Egulac lived well and were happy.

Background
This is a traditional story of the Nuu-chah-nulth people, who live along the west coast of Vancouver Island, Canada.

Plot
The two young hunters watched in amazement as the canoe came closer, and then, to their great surprise, the paddlers beached the canoe and came inland to the place where they themselves were hiding.  The elder of the two Nuu-chah-nulth men explained that he and his people were out hunting for seal pups, and asked the young hunters if they knew how to hunt seals.  They did not, so the elder offered to teach them.  The young men learned to hunt seals, and when the season was over, the Nuu-chah-nulth people left, as they had come.  The young men missed their new friends, and decided to go visit them the next year.  They did, and after that they often went with the Nuu-chah-nulth people to hunt seals and to learn more about them.  Eventually the young men became skilled seal hunters, and when the Nuu-chah-nulth people came to their area, they joined them in their canoe.  From then on, the two groups of hunters were friends, and often went hunting together.

Variants
This is one of a group of stories told by the Nuu-chah-nulth people about their relationships with the other tribes in the area.  In some stories, the visitors are from the Nootka tribe; in others, the Quatsinos.  In all of the stories, the young hunters learn from their visitors, and become friends.

Plot
The story takes place in the late 1800s. Two young men from the Kwakiutl tribe of the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America go out to hunt seals at night. While they are out, a thick fog rolls in and the calm is disturbed by the sound of war cries. The two young men fire at the figure that has appeared before them, only to discover that it is a woman. They realize that she is a shaman, or "trickster", who has taken on the role of a warrior to avenge the death of her husband, who was killed by white men. She tells them that the Black Robes are coming closer and closer to their land. The two young men are told by the woman to go to the village of their tribe and warn the elders of the approaching danger. The woman then disappears. The two young men return to their village and tell the elders of the warning they received. The elders decide to move their village to a new location. After some time, the young men go out hunting again, this time during the day. They are joined by the woman warrior, who has taken the form of a sea lion. She tells them that the Black Robes have brought smallpox to their land and many of their people have died. She warns them to be careful of the Black Robes and their "blue eyes".

Analysis
The story is an example of a type of oral literature called a "tale of the supernatural". It features a number of typical elements of this genre, including the use of a frame story, the setting (a distant place in the past), the presence of a monster, and the use of a moral or lesson. The story also makes use of a number of common themes, such as the brother-saving-brother theme and the idea of a supernatural helper.
The story also features a number of elements common to the oral literary tradition more broadly. For example, it makes use of repetition and formulaic language to aid in memorization and oral performance. It also makes use of a sparse, simple style of narration that leaves much to the imagination of the listener/reader.

"We are not afraid," said the young hunter.
"Then come here," said Klootchman, and he stepped out onto the shore. He was a tall man with a long white beard. He walked up to the young hunters and took one of their spears and threw it back into the water.
"Is that all you can do?" asked Klootchman. "Are you afraid?"
"No," said the young hunter, "we are not afraid."
"Then take my hand," said Klootchman, and he took one of the young hunter's hands in his own. "I will give you a gift," said Klootchman, and he took the other young hunter's hand in his own. "You will be my friends," said Klootchman, "and I will give you the gift of the sea. You will have fish and seals and salmon, and you will never be hungry."
From that day on, the two young hunters had a special relationship with Klootchman, and the spirit helped them on their hunts and kept them safe.

Suddenly they heard war cries and then firing.  They crawled to the water's edge and saw a battle scene in the moonlight.  It was a battle between the Yvon-Etches and the Pigans, two Iroquoian tribes.  The young Egulac men watched in silence until the hostiles had all gone home, and then they went home too. Variations
The story of the Battle of the Seven Islands, also known as the Battle of the Iroquoians, is a Canadian legend about a battle between the Iroquoian tribes of the Seven Nations.  The battle is said to have taken place on an island in the Saint Lawrence River, possibly in the area of Montreal.  The story says that the Iroquoians were driven from their villages and took refuge on the island, where they remained until they were starved out by the French.  The legend says that the Iroquoians were warriors and did not give up easily.  They fought the French with everything they had until they were all killed or starved.  The legend also says that the Iroquoians buried their dead warriors in the ground and that their graves are marked by flat stones.

Suddenly they heard a voice calling to them.  They returned the call and a man came walking towards them across the water.  When he reached the bank he asked them to go with him.  They consented and followed him to a large house.  Inside they found a number of other young men.  The man who had summoned them spoke to them about their future and the future of their people.  He told them that a great upheaval was coming.  They would be well to prepare for it by learning to read and write and to understand the white man's way of life.  He told them that their people were to be a bridge between the white and native people.  When they had learned all they could from the white man they were to return to their own people and teach them what they had learned.  The young men went back to their village and told their people of their experience.  They warned them of the coming upheaval and urged them to prepare for it.  The old people laughed at their words and told them that they did not understand.  The young men then went to the priest and asked him to teach them to read and write.  They also asked him many questions about the world and the universe.  The priest was amazed at their questions and their knowledge and told them that they were truly chosen.

Meanwhile, in another part of the world, a young man named Paddler was out hunting for food for his people.  He was out by himself when he was attacked by a wild animal.  The animal was about to kill him when a voice called out to it and it stopped.  The voice belonged to a spirit who had taken the form of a bird.  The spirit told Paddler that he was to go to the village and tell the people to prepare for a great upheaval.  The people laughed at Paddler and refused to believe his words.  They told him that if he could prove his words were true then they would believe him.  Paddler asked them for a sign and they told him to go to the river and look at the reflections of the trees on the water.  When he returned they asked him what he saw.  Paddler told them that the reflections were not the same as the trees themselves.  The people then believed his words and told him that they would prepare for the upheaval.

Suddenly a young woman appeared in the water and one of the hunters shot her.  The next morning the hunters found her body and it was so beautiful that they decided to take her home with them.  They cut off her head and put it in a bag, and when they got home they found that her head was alive and could talk.  They asked her to live with them, but she refused to talk to them unless they went back to the place where they had killed her and talked to her body.  They did this, and she spoke to them.  They asked her why she had come to the river, and she answered that she was looking for her husband.  The hunters asked her to live with them again, and this time she consented.  They lived together for a long time, and had a son whom they named Idi.  One day Idi went out hunting and came back with a woman he had found in the forest.  The woman was really a witch who had been sent by the mother of Idi's father-in-law to kill him.  The woman shot and killed Idi with a poisoned arrow, then she went up to the woman and cut off her head.  When the woman's head talked, it told the witch that she had killed her son.  The witch was frightened, and ran out of the house.  She went back to the place from which she had come, and when she got there the sun was rising.  It burned her up and turned her into a frog.

Analysis
This story is one of several in the ethnographic record which describe the acquisition of a wife who is a supernaturally endowed being.  The woman in this story is beautiful, able to talk when her head is severed from her body, and able to shoot game with a bow and arrow.  Her origin is supernatural, appearing in the water like a mermaid.  This woman is not a traditional wife, but rather a supernatural being who must be treated with great care.  Her acquisition is accompanied by a set of taboo rules, such as not hunting in the river, and not speaking to her unless asked a question.
The story also contains elements of a trickster tale, as the witch is outwitted by the woman's head.  The trickster in this case is not a traditional trickster figure

The young men saw a strange canoe heading for them and they did not realize that it was the spirit canoe of the Dead. The young men ran back to their own canoe and headed for home. When they reached home they found their village deserted and their people dead. The young men then realized that the fog and calm was caused by the spirits of the Dead blocking their path. They had died of smallpox brought by the white men. The young men then decided to paddle around the island to the place where their people had died. They saw a white man sitting in the place where the village had been. They approached him and he gave them gifts, and then they knew that he was a good spirit. The young men then went to their own village and found their people alive and healthy. They realized that the white man had given them the gift of the vaccine, which kept the people healthy. From then on, the young men went to the place where their people had died to get the vaccine from the white man, and after that, their people never died again.

Context
This story appears in J.R. Miller's 1916 collection of Native Canadian legends, The Hero Tales of the Algonkin People. Miller does not provide any notes or explanations for this particular story. As with all of the stories in the collection, the text is presented in a very simplified and condensed format, with little attention paid to such elements as tone, mood, and character development.

Analysis
This story can be analyzed as an example of the power of the white man, as seen through the eyes of a Native Canadian. In this story, the white man is able to give the gift of life through his vaccine, and he is therefore revered as a god-like figure. The story also shows the devastating effect that the white man's presence had on the Native Canadian population, as they were wiped out by diseases that the white men brought with them.

Themes
The story explores the themes of death, life, and the supernatural. It also explores the idea of the white man as a god-like figure, and shows the reverence that the Natives had for him.

Analysis
In this story, two young men go to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, one of them hears singing. At first, he thinks it is someone from the neighboring village, but when he pulls out his gun to shoot, he realizes that the singer is actually the moon. This realization fills the two men with joy.
The story can be interpreted in several ways. One possible interpretation is that the story is a commentary on the nature of violence. The two men are out by the water, hunting seals, which can be a dangerous activity. When one of them hears singing, he assumes that it is someone from a neighboring village, and pulls out his gun to shoot. However, he realizes that the singer is not another human being, but rather the moon. This realization brings the two men joy, and shows that violence is not the answer.
Another possible interpretation is that the story is about the connection between humans and nature. The two men are out by the water, and they are surrounded by the natural world. When one of them hears singing, he realizes that the singer is a part of the natural world as well. This realization brings the two men joy, and shows that humans are a part of nature, and should be in harmony with it.

Suddenly they heard a noise and looked around. In the distance they saw a canoe coming towards them. It was carrying two women. The young men were excited and asked where the seal hunters were. The women replied that they were not seal hunters, but had come to visit. The young men were disappointed and asked if the women knew where the seal hunters were. The women said no, but suggested that the young men go to the place where the seal hunter's uncle lived, as he might know. The young men went to the place where the uncle lived and asked him about the seal hunters. He told them that they had gone to the east to hunt seals. The young men were disappointed because they had wanted to go to the east to hunt seals themselves.

The women were impressed by the young men's desire to hunt seals, and one of them suggested that they go to the place where the seals were plentiful. The young men agreed, and the women helped them prepare their equipment. The young men were amazed that the women were such skilled hunters and were impressed by their courage. They travelled to the place where the seals were plentiful and successfully hunted seals all summer. In the fall the women returned to their own village, and the young men returned to theirs. The young men decided that they would like to marry the women, and asked their parents for permission. The parents agreed, and the young men and women were married. They lived happily ever after.

The End

One Night is a Canadian short film based on an old Ojibway legend about two young men who go out to hunt seals and end up bringing back two women instead. The film was written and directed by Kevin Lee Corbett, and produced by the National Film Board of Canada. The film stars Adam Beach, Lochlyn Munro, and Michelle Thrush.

The two young men were afraid and took refuge in a large old-growth red cedar tree that was on the bank of the river.  The tree had a large hollow section in its trunk that served as a perfect shelter from the river's strong currents and fog.

As the men sat in the tree, they heard a noise coming from outside. They peered through a crack in the tree and saw a large sea monster trying to pull the other men in the river to its death. The men in the tree tried to help their friends, but they were too far away.
As the sea monster continued to pull the men under the water, the two young men in the tree decided that they would rather die than be eaten by the monster. They climbed up as high as they could, and then held onto the tree's branches and let themselves be lifted up to the sky until they were out of reach of the monster.
The monster, not being able to reach them, gave up and left. The two young men climbed back down to the river bank, only to find that the monster had eaten both of their companions. They decided that they would rather live in the tree forever than go back down to the river.
And that's why, according to the Tla'amin legend, there are two young men who live in a red cedar tree, near the river, forever.

Suddenly they heard a voice calling across the water, "Will you two come over here?"

They answered back, "We are not allowed to leave our canoes."
Then came the reply, "I am Kwulukwala, the leader of all the seals."
They said, "We are not allowed to come to the shore."
"Then I will come out to you," said Kwulukwala, and soon the sound of seals barking was heard all around them.
"Are you Kwulukwala?" asked one of the young men.
"Yes," said the voice.
"Are you the leader of all the seals?"
"Yes."
"Then you must help us," said the young men. "We are not allowed to leave our canoes."
"Why not?" asked Kwulukwala.
"Because if we leave our canoes, we will be turned into stone."
"Then I will help you," said Kwulukwala. "But you must promise to give me half of the seal meat you catch in the future."
"We cannot make such a promise," said the young men. "We only hunt seals to feed our people. If we gave half of the meat to you, there would be none left for us."
"Then I will take only those seals that you do not use," said Kwulukwala.
"That is fair," said the young men.
So Kwulukwala helped them to catch many seals, and they were able to return home.
After that, every year when the young men went out to hunt seals, Kwulukwala would come down to the river and help them, and they became good friends.

The End.

The story of Kwulukwala is a traditional story of the Haida people. It is told by Roy Henry Vickers in his book "Raven Bringing the Light into the World" and by Tim Mack in his book "Trickster of the North".

Plot
The story is narrated by an Ojibwa elder who tells of two young hunters from the village of Egulac who go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, a fog comes down and they hear the noise of a canoe approaching. When they investigate, the occupants of the canoe ask them what they are doing there. The young men are frightened and do not understand how the people in the canoe could have arrived there so quickly in the fog. The elder explains that the canoeists were actually spirits who had come to warn the young men to be careful. After this, the young men return to the village and the elder tells the story to explain the importance of being cautious in life.

Variants
The story is a variant of the more widely known legend of the "Vanishing Canadians", which is found among various Native American tribes. The story of the "Vanishing Canadians" is also found in the works of the 19th century American writer Washington Irving. In his collection of essays The Adventures of Captain Bold, Irving writes about a group of explorers who encounter a tribe of Native Americans in the Canadian wilderness. The explorers stop at a Native American village to trade and while they are there, all of the Native Americans disappear overnight. The explorers leave the village and never learn the reason for the disappearance of the Native Americans. Irving suggests that the Native Americans may have been spirits who only appeared to the explorers as a vision.

The film is based on the 1965 book The Ballad of Big John by John A. MacDonald and Colin Low. They reply, "We are here." "You are on Vancouvers's island," said the voice. "How is that possible, said the young men, "when we are on the mainland?" Production
The short film was produced in 1940 by the Canadian government as a part of a wartime propaganda campaign to boost morale and promote national unity. The story is based on a legend told by the Kwakwaka'wakw people, an indigenous group located on the west coast of Canada. The film was shot at Alert Bay on the west coast of Canada.

Reception
The film was screened at the 11th Academy Awards in 1939 as part of the short subjects category. It was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Short Subject (One-Reel).

Themes
The story is about how humans should respect nature and not always take from it without asking. It also shows that animals and nature have spirits that should be respected.

There are many variations of this story. In some versions, the two young men are out hunting and come across a beautiful woman. They approach her and she turns into the sea monster and kills them. In other versions, the beast is a whale and the young men are out hunting seals. Regardless of the variations, the story always shows respect for nature and the spirits of the land and water.

Suddenly they heard a voice calling across the water, "Is it you, Wandering Spirit?" They saw a figure coming towards them, and it was a woman in a canoe. She was a goddess, and she gave them a gift of two stones that would protect them always.

Synopsis
The two young men go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, a woman goddess appears and gives them two stones that will protect them always.

Background
The story is from the Kwakwáká'waḱw (Kwakiutl) people of the northwest coast of North America. The Kwakwáká'waḱw have a complex system of mythology that is used to explain the world around them. The stories are performed as dances and are accompanied by singing and the use of carved masks.

Analysis
This story can be analyzed in many ways, including:

Sociological - the story may have been used to explain the creation of the world.
Psychological - the two young men represent the inner self of each person.
Religious - the story is part of a larger mythology used by the Kwakwáká'waḱw to explain the world around them.
Literary - the use of a goddess to convey the idea of a higher power has been used in many stories throughout history.

The young men saw a canoe approaching them and they called out to the occupants and were surprised to find that it was their two friends from upriver. The four young men decided to hunt together the next day and set up camp on a nearby island for the night.
In the morning they set out in their canoes to hunt and came upon a large seal herd. They chased the seals into a narrow cove and were able to kill as many as they wanted. After they had killed a sufficient number of seals, they returned to their camp and began to prepare their meal.
As they were sitting there, a young woman walked up to them and said that she was the spirit of the island and had come to warn them that they were in danger. They should return to their homes immediately. The young men laughed at her and told her to stop bothering them.
The young woman became angry and summoned a storm that almost sank their canoes. The young men were forced to swim to the island and the young woman helped them to shore. She explained to them that she had warned them because she loved them and did not want them to die.
The young men were converted to a new way of thinking and returned to their homes. They decided to devote themselves to the service of their people and to the protection of their land.

Themes
The story is an example of a common theme in Tlingit literature. It demonstrates the Tlingit belief in the power of the natural world and the importance of respecting the spirits that control that power. It also shows the Tlingit belief in the power of love and the ability of that power to change people's lives.

Cultural significance
This story is an example of a genre of Tlingit literature called "the old-time stories." These stories are used to convey important cultural, historical, and philosophical information to younger generations. They are also used to explain the origin of certain customs and traditions.

The young men were afraid, but they were not afraid any more, and they sang with the others.
The next morning the young men went back to the place where they had heard the singing, but nothing happened. Just then one of them picked up a stone and threw it into the water, and immediately the singing was heard again. The young men were afraid, and they ran away. They never told anyone what had happened, for they were afraid.
After that the young men never went seal hunting at night, for they were afraid of the singing that came from the water.

The Source of the Story
The story was told by an informant to Franz Boas in 1902. Boas recorded it in The Serials of the Kwaksiutl Indians as part of his research on the culture and folklore of the Kwakwaka'wakw people. The story was not published until 1935, in The Journal of American Folklore, in an issue dedicated to Boas's work.

The Story's Significance
This tale is an example of a Kwakwaka'wakw serial, a type of story in which a series of unrelated events are connected by a common theme. In this story, the theme is the inevitability of death. The events are connected by the speakers' speculation as to the cause of each event in the chain. The story also deals with the idea that everything in the world is interconnected.

Background
The story comes from the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) people of the northwest coast of North America.  It is a common theme among the indigenous peoples of the northwest coast that a person can travel to the land of the dead and return.  In this story, the two young men go to the land of the moon, where they have a wonderful time, and then return to their village.  The story may also be interpreted as a mythological explanation of the origin of the potlatch feast.  The potlatch is a traditional feast of the indigenous peoples of the northwest coast of North America.  The potlatch is a communal feast at which the host gives away as much of his wealth as he can.  The potlatch is a very old tradition, going back at least 13,000 years.  The potlatch was outlawed by the Canadian government from 1884 to 1951, because it was thought that it was responsible for the impoverishment of the indigenous peoples.  Today, the potlatch is an important part of the indigenous cultures of the northwest coast.

Description
The Rogue Wave is a 1954 Canadian short documentary film directed by Colin Low and Wolf Koenig. It was produced for the National Film Board of Canada and is narrated by Pierre Berton. The film recounts the story of two Native American men from the village of Egulac on the Columbia River who were swept out to sea and drowned by a rogue wave. The film was shot on location at the Columbia River bar using dramatic reenactment footage and archival material. The Rogue Wave was part of the NFB's Pacificanada series, which showcased the west coast of Canada and the United States in 15-minute films.

Production
In October 1953, Colin Low and Wolf Koenig went to Astoria, Oregon to begin production on a film about the Columbia River. Low and Koenig decided to use a 16 mm motion picture camera to shoot dramatic reenactment footage of the events that led to the deaths of the two Native American men. Low and Koenig's original plan was to use the film to dramatize the story of the two men and the Rogue Wave that killed them. However, while in Astoria, Low and Koenig decided to change the focus of the film to tell the story of the Columbia River bar and the many lives lost to the waters off the coast of Oregon and Washington.The film's narrator, Pierre Berton, described the Rogue Wave as "the last and greatest of all the wave monsters."

Reception
The Rogue Wave was premiered on October 20, 1954, in Vancouver, British Columbia. The film was well received and went on to win several awards, including a Canadian Film Award for Best Direction and a Canadian Screen Award for Best Sound Recording. The film was also selected for screening at the 1955 Cannes Film Festival.

Suddenly they heard a noise and looked up and saw a huge boulder falling towards them. They tried to run but it was too late and they were crushed by the rock.

Plot
This myth is about two young men who go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, the weather turns foggy and calm. Suddenly, they hear a loud noise and look up just in time to see a boulder falling towards them. No matter how hard they try to run away, they cannot escape and are eventually crushed by the rock.

Variants
This myth can be found among the Nuu-chah-nulth peoples living along the west coast of Vancouver Island. The story can vary from telling of two men, two women, or even a man and a woman who are crushed by the rock. In some versions, the boulder is not simply a large rock, but rather a giant sent by the tide-being to punish the hunters for disturbing his domain.

Analysis
This myth can be analyzed as a warning to people not to go out to the sea to hunt seals at night, or during bad weather conditions. It also highlights the power of the natural world and the dangers of underestimating that power.

Background
The story of "The Canoe" is one of many collected by Ursula Le Guin from the Kwakwáká'waḱ people of the Pacific Northwest. Like many of Le Guin's retellings, her version is true to the original story, but is also true to Le Guin's belief in the power of storytelling. The story is included in the collection Dancing at the Edge of the World, and is one of Le Guin's favorites from all her works.

Synopsis
Two young hunters from Egulac go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there a fog comes down and it becomes calm. Suddenly they hear a noise and look up and see a big canoe coming towards them. They are afraid it is the ghost of a man who was drowned there many years before. The canoe comes very close and the hunters can see it is loaded with seal fur. Finally it stops and a man gets out. It turns out to be a man from Egulac who had gone away long ago and had been dead for many years. He had come back to tell the hunters how to hunt seals.

Variants
This story has been variously retitled by Le Guin as "The Ghost Canoe", "The Canoe from the Dead", and "The Seal Hunters".

Themes
The story is about the power of the dead and the power of storytelling. The two are connected in that the dead can only communicate with the living through stories.

The young men saw the fog come in and cover up the land. When it had covered everything, it rolled up the sides of the hills, and covered up the land all over. Then it rolled down to the water's edge and up the other side of the hill again. After that the young men heard a great noise behind them and saw a large herd of caribou coming down the mountain.
Intrigued, they followed the caribou to their hiding place, where they saw that the entire herd was pregnant. The young men then realized that the fog had covered the land to make a new world, and the caribou had come to see their new calves. After this the young men returned to their village, where they told of their adventure.

The legend
This legend is one of many told by the Tlingit people of the northwest coast of North America. It is a story of the creation of the world, and is similar to other creation myths from around the world.

Variants
This legend has many variants, depending on who tells it. In one variant, the two young men are out hunting for food. In another, they are just out for a walk. In some stories, the two young men are actually one man, who catches a glimpse of his own reflection in the water and is so amazed by it that he falls in and drowns. In this version, the caribou come to mourn the man, and when they see the young man's wife, they ask her to climb a mountain and sing a certain song. She climbs the mountain and sings, and as she sings, the caribou turn into people.

The tale today
The legend of the two young men from Egulac is not told very often today, but it is still remembered by some Tlingit people. It is one of many stories that make up the Tlingit cultural heritage.

Plot
The two young men from Egulac were out hunting for seals when a fog came in and they decided to return home. As they traveled through the forest, they heard strange noises. Suddenly, a large white man appeared in the middle of the path. The young men were afraid, but the white man did not harm them. Instead, he spoke to them in their own language and told them that he was also afraid in the dark. The young men then realized that the white man was alone and afraid as well. The two young men invited the white man to travel with them to their village, and he agreed. When they arrived at the village, the chief of the tribe was pleased that they had brought a new member to their people. The two young men and the white man then lived together in the village.

The white man chases after them and catches them. He speaks to them in their language, telling them that he is also afraid in the dark. As they were returning home, they met with a terrible accident. One of the men drowned and the other was so frightened that he jumped into the water and was drowned also. This is the story of the Egulac tragedy, as it is called by the Kwakiutl Native Americans of the British Columbia coast. It is a story that has been told many times and is known to most Kwakiutl. It is a story that is full of tragedy and sadness, and it is a story that is full of the supernatural.

Story
The two young men who were involved in the Egulac tragedy were named Tlelo and Wadzus. They were very good friends and spent most of their time together. One night they decided to go down to the river to hunt seals. They had been very successful on previous trips, and they were confident that they would be successful on this trip as well. As they were returning home, the weather suddenly changed. It became foggy and calm. The water was as smooth as glass, and the forest was shrouded in fog. Suddenly, without warning, Tlelo's canoe capsized and he was drowned. Wadzus tried to save his friend, but he was too frightened. He jumped into the water and was also drowned.
The Kwakiutl believe that when someone dies, their spirit goes on a journey to the land of the dead. However, the spirits of those who die tragically or violently are prevented from entering the land of the dead. Instead, they are forced to wander around in the land of the living. This is what happened to Tlelo and Wadzus. Their spirits could not enter the land of the dead, so they continue to wander around the Egulac River.
The Kwakiutl believe that it is dangerous to travel at night, especially near the Egulac River. This is because they believe that the spirits of Tlelo and Wadzus are always around, looking for young men to join them. They believe that if a young man is out at night near the Egulac River, he may be offered a ride in a canoe by one of the spirits. If he gets into the canoe, he will drown and join the spirits in their eternal journey.

The young men saw the fog coming towards them and they started to run. The fog overtook them and one of them was turned into a deer. This is the story that opens Regina producer Don Hodges' 1979 documentary Fog of Love.

Synopsis
Fog of Love is a 56-minute documentary film that tells the story of two Cree boys from the reserve of Egulac, near Fort Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan, who go down to the Qu'Appelle River to hunt seals. While they are there, the fog rolls in and one of the boys turns into a deer. The film is based on a Cree folktale, and it is told through a combination of live action and animation. The live action was shot on location in Saskatchewan, featuring local actors and dancers. The animation was created by the National Film Board of Canada's animation studio, under the direction of Yves Dion, and it is based on the drawings of Cree artist Alex Janvier. The film was made for $118,000.

Production
Fog of Love was the idea of Regina producer Don Hodges, who had been looking for a story to tell for some time. The film was made in collaboration with the National Film Board of Canada. Hodges approached the NFB after seeing a film they made called The Silence of the Sea, which was about the tides. He wanted to make a film about the prairies, and the NFB suggested he go to Saskatchewan to find a story. Hodges went to the Native Arts and Crafts Centre in Saskatoon, where he met Cree artist Alex Janvier, who agreed to work on the project. Hodges also met a Cree elder who told him the story of the two boys and the fog, which became the basis of the film. The live action was shot in the summer of 1978, using local actors and dancers. The animation was created in Montreal, based on Janvier's drawings. The music was created by Regina musician David Gerry, whose 1977 album Northern Lights was a collection of contemporary music inspired by the North.

Reception
Fog of Love received a Genie Award nomination

The sea serpent is also believed to be a guardian of the sea and the fish that live in the sea.

Further information
This story is a traditional Cree tale.  It is a classic example of a "trickster tale," a genre of folklore found all over the world.  The trickster is a mischievous character who plays tricks on other characters in the story, but in doing so he always seems to get himself into more trouble.  In this story the two young men are tricked by the prairie dogs, but in the end it is the prairie dogs who are dancing with the young men.  This story is also an example of the "animal story" genre.  Animal stories are tales in which animals play the leading roles.  In this story the animals are prairie dogs.  Prairie dogs are small burrowing animals that live in the prairies of North America. The young men saw a light in the distance and headed towards it.  They were surprised to see it was the SS Henk, a ship that had been wrecked only a short time before on the sandbar at the mouth of the Fraser River.  The ship was on fire and the young men watched as the crew abandoned ship and swam to safety.  The young men later returned with their father to recover valuables from the ship.  The SS Henk was a St. Roch-class steamship that was built in 1911 and wrecked on November 12, 1913.

Production
The story of the SS Henk is told through the performance of three actors in a theatre in the round.  The production uses masks, mime, music and storytelling to bring the story to life.  The production is designed to appeal to both young audiences and adults.

History
The play was first performed in 1976 at the Arts and Culture Centre in Vancouver, British Columbia.  It was written by George Ryga and directed by Ron Trainer.  The play was revived in 1982 by the Gateway Theatre in Richmond, British Columbia.

Background
The Wenatchee was a side-wheel steamboat that was built in 1861 in Portland, Oregon. It was owned by the Oregon Steam Navigation Company and was one of the company's most important boats. The boat was 133 feet (40 m) long and 23 feet (7 m) wide, with a tonnage of 200 tons. It had a crew of 25 men and could carry up to 300 passengers. It was powered by a 50 horsepower (37 kW) steam engine. The boat regularly traveled between The Dalles and Portland, Oregon, carrying passengers and freight. On May 15, 1870, the Wenatchee was traveling from The Dalles to Portland when it hit a rock and sank. All of the passengers and crew survived, but the boat was a total loss.

Influence
The story of the Wenatchee's sinking is told in the 1930 novel Cannonball by Joseph Robinette. The story was also the inspiration for the 1965 Walt Disney Productions film Seconds to Live, produced by Ron Wager and directed by James L. Conway. The film stars Jeffrey Hunter, Frances Farmer, and William Hopper.

The Chilcotin people live in the central interior of British Columbia, and their territory extends from the Chilcotin Plateau in the west to the Fraser River in the east, and from the Coast Mountains in the south to the Yukon-Alaska boundary in the north.

Suddenly a young woman appeared in the fog and she sang a song and then she was changed into a seal and dived into the water.  The two young men shot at her and she was killed.  They cut open her body and found she was full of pearls.  They took the pearls to the village and traded them for women and furs.  The two young men who had gone out to hunt seal were Egle and Nootka.

Context
The myth was collected by Franz Boas in 1905 from an informant whose name is not recorded.  It comes from the Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) people of the northwest coast of North America.  Boas published it in 1906 in Handbook of American Indians North of Mexico, volume 1, in the section on the Kwakiutl.  The version above is a translation of the original German.  Boas's informant had learned German in mission school, so he was able to communicate directly with Boas in that language.

Analysis
The myth is a variant of the more widespread Northwest Coast seal woman myth.  In this myth a young man goes out hunting and encounters a seal woman.  He kills her, and is then visited by her ghost who demands revenge.  In this version Egle and Nootka avoid this fate by giving the seal woman's body to the tribe, and thus sharing her with everyone.  This ensures that she will not return to haunt them.  The myth can be seen as an explanation for the origin of pearls, and also as a story about the acquisition of women and wealth.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. As they sat in their canoe, a young woman appeared in front of them. She sang and danced in the moonlight. The young men were enchanted by her and did not notice that she was putting spells on them.
The young woman was actually a witch who had been waiting for centuries to have the power to turn men into seals. When the young men awoke the next morning, they found that they had been turned into seals. They were unable to speak and could only make noises that sounded like the bleating of sheep.
The two young men lived for a long time in the water, unable to return to their village. They were eventually killed by the Haida, who used their fur to make clothing and blankets. The young woman who had enchanted them was also killed. Her head was cut off and placed in a box, which was buried in the ground.

The story
This story was collected by Franz Boas from an oral narrator in the late 19th century. The narrator was a member of the Tlingit tribe. The story is similar to other tales from the Pacific Northwest. The story of the two young men who were turned into seals is found in the folklore of many cultures around the world.

Interpretation
In this tale, the young woman represents the power of nature. She has the power to turn humans into seals, the animal that provides the fur they need to survive in the rainy climate of the Pacific Northwest. The young men represent the carelessness of youth. They do not take the power of nature seriously and pay the price for their lack of respect.

Context and sources
The story of the two young men who were turned into seals is found in the folklore of many cultures around the world. It has been collected from many Native American tribes in the Pacific Northwest. The story is found in Boas's 1895 publication, "The Journal of American Folk-Lore," in the article, "Further Notes on the Tlingit Language and Folk-Lore."

Interpretation
The story "One Night" is a Canadian legend about a mythical sea-going people called the "Sons of the Sea" or "Sons of the Morning." The story tells of two young men from a coastal village who go on a journey and eventually encounter a ship. The story is used by anthropologists to trace the distribution of Aboriginal tribes along the west coast of Canada.

The young men saw a canoe approaching and heard someone call out 'Tsisghemew!' It was the ghost of Tsisghemew, a man who had been drowned many years before while hunting seals. The young men were terrified and rowed back to the shore as fast as they could. When they reached their camp they told the others what had happened.

The next night two young women went down to the river to collect berries. While they were there it became foggy and calm. Suddenly they heard someone calling 'Tsisghemew!' It was the ghost of Tsisghemew. The young women were terrified and ran back to the village as fast as they could. When they reached the chief's house they told the others what had happened.
The chief then went down to the river alone. When he reached the spot where Tsisghemew had drowned, he called out 'Tsisghemew!' The ghost appeared and the chief spoke to it. Tsisghemew told the chief that he could only rest because the place where he had drowned was now polluted by the white man's rubbish. The chief was very sorry. He asked Tsisghemew what he could do to help. Tsisghemew told him that if he and his people collected all the rubbish and put it in a special place then Tsisghemew would be happy and could rest.
The people of Egulac worked for many days collecting the rubbish and putting it in a special place. When they had finished Tsisghemew's ghost appeared to the chief again. He thanked the chief and told him that he was now happy and could rest. From that day on the place where Tsisghemew had drowned was known as 'The Place of Restless Spirits'.

The young men got into their canoe and rowed as fast as they could toward the shore, but the monster followed them and they could hear its breath behind them. When they looked back the monster was blocking the way to the shore. One of the young men picked up his spear and threw it at the monster, which made a noise like a bell being struck. The monster disappeared and the young men rowed to the shore. They got out of the canoe and went into the bushes to hide, and the monster did not come back.

The story of "The Great Sea Serpent" is one of several Native American legends about lake monsters and sea serpents, including Nessie and Champ. It is also one of several legends about monsters that block the way to the afterlife, including the Norse Bounder.

Suddenly they heard a voice calling: "Egoyan! Egoyan!" It was the voice of Hoyo the Great, the chief of all the Lelcoh people. They were so frightened that they hid behind a tree. Then they heard another voice, and it was the voice of the Great Chief Wah-mah-nee of all the Iroquoians. "Egoyan! Egoyan!" said he. "What is the matter?" asked the two young men. "We are to be the chiefs of all the Iroquoians," said Hoyo the Great. "We will give you the laws of the Iroquoians," said the Great Chief Wah-mah-nee. So the two young men went back to their village, and they told the people what had happened. "From this day forward," said the people, "you are the chiefs of the Iroquoians, and you must make the laws for us." And from that day forward, the Two Row Wampum was made, and it is the law between the Iroquoians and the people of the sea.

The Two-Row Wampum is a belt of wampum beads, representing an agreement between the Iroquoian peoples and the maritime peoples of the eastern seaboard of North America, in which the Iroquoians acknowledged the maritime peoples' right to fish and hunt in the waters along the Atlantic coast, while the maritime peoples acknowledged the Iroquoians' right to occupy the lands upland from the Atlantic coast. The name comes from the two rows of beads in the belt, one row representing the land, the other the water.
The Two-Row Wampum is sometimes confused with the Dancing with the White Man picture wampum, which represents a different agreement made by the Iroquoian confederacy with European settlers.

The young men saw a light in the distance and they rowed towards it. When they reached the shore, they went into a hall where they saw a number of women sitting on mats. The women were singing and their voices were like the voices of waves. The young men were welcomed by the women, and they were given marijuana to smoke. The young men became very high and they began to feel that they were in a dream. The women gave them a special kind of salmon to eat, and after they had eaten, the young men began to feel that they were transformed into something else. The women then gave them a special kind of root to chew on, and the young men began to feel that they were in a trance.
The young men then began to see serpents all around them. The serpents were the guardians of the women, and they were not to be afraid of them. The young men were then given some berries to eat, and after they had eaten, they began to feel that they were in a canoe. The women then gave them some hallucinogenic snuff to sniff, and the young men began to see strange visions. The women told the young men that they were now ready to return to their own people, and they gave them some marijuana to take with them. The young men then rowed back to their own people, and when they arrived, they told them all about the women and the hall of the Women of the Copper Sun.

Analysis
This myth is one of several that tell of the transformation of young men into something else. In this case, the young men are transformed into seals, or at least, they believe that they are seals. The transformation is not a permanent one, and it serves to reinforce the idea that the young men are now ready to take on the roles of adults in their society. The marijuana and other hallucinogens that the young men are given serve to help them in their transformation, and they are also given food that will help them to see visions. The women who live in the hall are seen as powerful beings, and they are the guardians of the young men's transformation.

Variants
This myth is found in slightly different versions in other works by Boas, including "The Social Organization of the Kwakiutl" and "Tsimshian Mythology."

The Wind-Born Woman is a traditional Ojibwe legend told by the people of the Great Lakes region.  It is one of a series of legends told by the Ojibwe about the spirits of the natural world.  In this legend the spirits of the wind are personified as a woman who becomes the mistress of a man from the shore.  The legend can be interpreted as a tale of the power of nature and the futility of trying to control the wind.

Suddenly they heard a loud noise and a great flame leaped up. An enormous steamship was passing through the narrows. The force of the current carried the two young men underwater to the bottom. They held their breath and struggled to the surface. When they got there, they saw that the ship had struck an underwater rock and had broken in two. The young men swam to shore and ran to a nearby village to warn the people.

The ship was the RMS Empress of Ireland, which sank on July 10, 1914, after striking the rock in the St. Lawrence River, near Quebec City, killing 353 of her 469 passengers and crew. The ship was en route from Liverpool, England to Montreal, Quebec.

The two young men who warned the village were Oskanaade'i (also spelled Oskana-de-i, "He-Whom-They-Call-At-the-Edge-Of-The-Village") and Poi-Ka-Wa-Ka-Wa-Ka-Ya-O-Ka-Ya-Ka-O ("He-Who-Is-Really-Scared-Of-The-Wild-Beasts"). They were the last recorded eyewitnesses to the sinking of the Empress of Ireland.

Their account was recorded by Father Marie-Victorin, a priest who lived in the nearby mission of Saint-François-Xavier. Father Victorin had been sent by the Catholic Church to minister to the Indigenous peoples living along the St. Lawrence River.

The two young men's account of the sinking of the Empress of Ireland was first published in 1925 in the book The Last Voyage of the Empress of Ireland by Charles A. Hitsman. Hitsman was a historian and the curator of the Maritime History Collection at the National Library of Canada.

The account of the two young men was later recounted in the 1997 book The Ship That Died of Shame by Roger Crowley. Crowley wrote that the sinking of the Empress of Ireland was "the greatest maritime disaster in Canadian history."

This story is an example of a common motif in the oral literature of the Pacific Northwest. Through his detailed description of the events, the narrator creates a situation in which the reader feels sympathy for the young men. Possible origin
This myth is related to the Tlingit people. The Tlingit live in the Pacific Northwest in the United States and Canada. Their legend says that a long time ago, the world was covered by ice. When the ice melted, the Raven brought out the sun, moon, and stars. After that, the Tlingit people lived in peace. However, one day a terrible sea monster came and destroyed the peace. The Tlingit people were afraid to go out and hunt seals. Two young men decided to go out and hunt seals. When they were out on the water, they saw the monster. The monster was so big that it was blocking the sun. The young men were afraid, but they remembered what the Raven had done for them. They decided to fight the monster. The young men shot the monster in the heart and killed it. After that, the Tlingit people gave the two young men the name of 'Heroes'.

The young men saw a strange light in the distance and went toward it. When they came to the bank of a lagoon they saw that it was a fire built by the Tillamooks, a tribe of people who lived beyond the lagoon.  The young men were afraid to go back to their canoes and try to return to their village, so they decided to spend the night where they were.  The Tillamooks saw the smoke from the young men's fire and came down to investigate.  When they saw the women in the group, they decided to seize them and take them back to their village as wives.  The young men were powerless to prevent this, and spent the winter as the guests of the Tillamooks.  Eventually, the young men were allowed to return to their own people, and they brought back with them a wife for the chief of their tribe.  This is the story of how the Tillamooks came to have fair-haired people among them.

Variation in telling
There are several variations to this story. In one version, the Tillamooks mistake the white men for gods, and build an altar for them to sleep on. In another version, the Tillamooks are so impressed by the white men's guns that they all want to have one, and the white men agree to make them guns in exchange for the women. In yet another version, the white men are so impressed by the beauty of the Tillamook women that they take many of them as wives, and later return to get more.

Real history
The first white men to come to the area were probably John Meares in 1788, but the first long-term European presence was the Hudson's Bay Company post at Fort George, established in 1834. The Tillamooks were driven out of their lands by the white settlers, and many moved to reservations. In 1856, a smallpox epidemic decimated the Tillamook people, and many more died in subsequent years as their land was gradually taken from them.

They thought at first it was only the reflection of the moonlight on the water, but soon perceived that it was canoe really and that there were several men in it. The boat came up to within a few feet of them, and then one of the men in it called out in the Ojibway language, "Put up your guns, we are only passing through." They were members of the Métis people, who were traders and hunters connected with the Hudson Bay Company. After the canoe had passed on, the two young men from Egulac went on with their hunt, and soon after they had shot a seal, heard the news that the Métis were encamped not far off. They went to the camp, and spent the day in amusement with their friends, and the next morning started for their own home. About midday they met a party of Métis coming from the other side, and after exchanging greetings they went on their way. When they reached the place where they had killed the seal, they found that it had been carried away by the tide, and they did not know what to do. While they were standing and talking about it, one of the Métis who was in the party came up to them and said, "I see you are troubled about your seal. I will give you some advice. You are young men and not strong, and it is no use your trying to carry that heavy load. Let us take it to your village for you, and you give us half of it. What do you say?" They thought this was a very reasonable proposal, and accepted it. The Métis took the seal, and carried it to their own camp, and then cut it in two and dried it. After a few days they brought half of it to the young men, and gave them the other half also. When the young men from Egulac got home, they related their adventure, and the kindness of the Métis, and said, "We must always remember that the Métis are our friends."

This story is another example of how in the old Haida culture, everything in life was interconnected and nothing was ever really left to chance. Suddenly they heard a noise and looked up and saw a huge sea monster coming out of the water. It was the Nagapanaq, the beast of the sea. It was so big that it blocked out the moon. The young men got scared and ran away.

Interpretation
The story of the Nagapanaq is a common one among the Kwakiutl and other Northwest Coast peoples. It is a story of a dangerous and fearsome creature that lives in the sea and can be encountered by hunters. The story is told in the context of a potlatch, a feast and ceremonial gift-giving event. The story is told by a hereditary chief to demonstrate his right to rule and to show the wealth and power of his family.
The story also has a historical context. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the potlatch was outlawed by the Canadian government as a means of trying to assimilate the First Nations peoples of the northwest coast into European Canadian culture. The stories told during the potlatch were recorded by anthropologists and ethnographers, and many of these stories are the only surviving records of important cultural traditions.

Plot
This story takes place in the past along the shores of Lake Superior. Two young men from Egulac go down to the river to hunt seals. While they are there, a noise in the water causes one of them to wonder what it is. His companion tells him it is only a seal. Suddenly a water-spout rises up and a great fish appears. The two young men run to their canoes and paddle to shore. When they look back, the great fish is still following them. They take their guns and shoot at it, but it is no good. It is a windigo.

Variants
There are several variants of this story, including one that takes place in the far north where the Inuit hunt walrus. In this version, the windigo is described as a giant walrus.

Symbolism
The windigo is a monster that appears in many Algonquin stories. It is said to be an evil spirit that feeds on human flesh. In this story, the windigo is a giant fish that follows the two young men home. They are unable to kill it, and it is only by the intervention of the Old Man (who is also known as the Great Spirit) that they are finally saved.

Origins
This story has been passed down through the generations by the Ojibwa people. It is one of many stories that tell of the power of the windigo.

The legend of the Two Young Men of Egulac is one of several tales featuring the people of Egulac, a village located on the north shore of the Fraser River, west of Fort Langley. The site of the village was at the confluence of the Fraser and the Harrison rivers, at what is now known as Stoney Creek.The Egulac people spoke a Salishan language, possibly a Coast Salish dialect related to the Stó:lō dialects spoken to the east of the Fraser River. The Egulac people were not among the signatories of the Douglas Treaties of 1850–1854, and their land was not ceded. They were among the last indigenous peoples in British Columbia to have contact with Europeans.

The legend is told in Iscootch: Tales of the Fraser River People, a collection of Native stories of the Fraser River region, edited by Robert A. Jouet and published in 1990 by the BC Provincial Museum.

On the most obvious level, it is about two hunters who go out to hunt seals, but one of them decides to go home, although he changes his mind several times. The repetition of the idea that the first hunter has gone home, when he really hasn't, is a common trickster device, and is found in many stories around the world.  The story can also be interpreted as a dream narrative, in which the two hunters represent different aspects of the dreamer's psyche.  The first hunter might represent the conscious mind, which is trying to make up its mind to do something, while the second hunter represents the unconscious mind, which knows what the conscious mind is thinking and feels neglected.  The repetition of the first hunter's decision to go home can be seen as the conscious mind's attempts to rationalize its decisions.  The story can also be seen as a comment on the nature of reality and perception.  The fact that the first hunter goes home even though he says he doesn't, can be seen as a comment on the fluidity of reality, and the fact that what we perceive as real is often a matter of interpretation.

Background
This story is from the Kwakiutl people of the northwest coast of America. The Kwakiutl are a branch of the Coast Salish peoples. They are known for their elaborate dances and potlatch feasts. Overview
The Black Hills are considered a sacred place by many Native American tribes. In 1874, gold was discovered in the Black Hills, and thousands of miners rushed to the area. This led to conflict with the Native Americans who considered the Black Hills their ancestral homeland.
The Great Sioux War of 1876 was fought over the Black Hills. After the United States won the war, the Black Hills were never returned to the Great Sioux Nation.
The story of the Black Hills is one of the longest-running legal cases in U.S. history. The Ponca Tribe of Nebraska, one of the tribes that were forced to move from the Black Hills, has been fighting in court to regain the land ever since.

Context
The story is part of the Tlingit and Haida traditions of the Pacific Northwest. It is one of a group of stories known as the "Tale of the Two Young Men", which are also found among the Kwakiutl, Heiltsuk, and Nuu-chah-nulth. The story was collected by Franz Boas in 1895 from an informant who had heard it from his grandmother.

Analysis
The story is an example of a genre of oral literature known as the "Tale of the Two Young Men", which are found throughout the indigenous cultures of the Americas. The story contains elements of the supernatural, including the creation of fog and calm, as well as the ability of the young men to disappear. The story also contains elements of the trickster genre, with the two young men acting in a trickster-like manner, playing on the idea of knowledge and the lack thereof. The story also contains a great deal of ambiguity, with the young men's actions and motivations being open to interpretation, and the narrative itself being open to multiple readings.

The film was shot in August 1973 in Bella Coola, British Columbia. The ship in the film is the SS Skeena, which did in fact sink in 1914, but not in the waters off of Bella Coola.

Release
The film premiered at the Vancouver International Film Festival in October 1973.

Reception
The film won the Best Short Film Award at the festival.

Suddenly they heard a sound, and a great many little fish leaped into the air at the same time. They knew that this was the time when the seal people came up from under the water to look at the human beings, and that they must not look at them directly or they would be turned into stone. So the young men crept down to the water's edge and lay there on their stomachs, looking at the seal people as they came up in the air.
Then the young men saw that the seal people were playing ball with a small round ball, and they wished very much to join in the game. But they knew that they must not make a noise or the seal people would go away and they would be sorry. So they tried to think of something to do to amuse themselves while they were lying there. One of them took up a pebble and began to throw it along the beach, but soon he heard the other one's footsteps running away. Then he knew that he had been changed into a seal, and that the other young man had gone home and told his people that the fish were biting at the other side of the river. So he went home, too, and when he got there he saw that it was daylight, and he wondered how it could be day already when he had only closed his eyes for a moment. Then he knew that he had been turned into a seal, and that he would live in the water from that time on.

The source of this story is uncertain. It has been collected from the Kwakiutl and the Tlingit.

Suddenly they heard a voice upstream calling "Egoy!" and then another voice downstream calling "Egoy!" The two men were puzzled and afraid. They crawled into the willows to hide and saw four figures coming down the river in a canoe. The figures were dressed in fox furs and had long horns on their heads. They pulled their canoe onto the bank, and one of them spoke to the two young men in the Egulac language.
The young men recognized the voice of the chief of the mountain people. He told them that he and his three sons had gone up the mountain to hunt the Wind River Grizzly, but they had angered the grizzly and it had killed two of the party. The chief asked the young men to help him get his sons back to their village. The young men agreed and they set out in the canoe.
As they traveled downriver, they heard a loud noise behind them and saw a great grizzly bear running along the top of the cliffs. The chief explained that this was the Wind River Grizzly, the most powerful grizzly in the world, and it was angry because they had killed its cubs.
They traveled on for four days and nights, and at last they saw the village of the mountain people. The young men helped the chief bury his sons, and then they went back to their own village.
The young men told the people of Egulac about the mountain people and their powerful chief. From then on, the people of Egulac lived in peace with the mountain people, and the Wind River Grizzly left them alone.

Suddenly they heard a voice calling to them. They saw a figure standing on the water, and then another, and another, and they knew that it was the spirits of their dead fathers calling to them. The young men were Afraid, and they ran home to the reservation and told the head man what had happened. The head man said that the young men had dreamed correctly, and that the old people would go to the river and build a scaffold, and they would climb up and look at the stars and sing all night.
The next night, the old people went down to the river and built a scaffold, and climbed up and looked at the stars all night. And the young men who had dreamed it all, they were the only ones who knew that the old people were really looking at the stars for the spirits of their fathers.

Analysis
This story is an example of a type of dream story that is common in Native American literature. It deals with the idea of the dream as a sort of spiritual experience, and as a way of communicating with the dead. In this story, the dream is a way of bridging the gap between the living and the dead, and serves to strengthen the beliefs of the characters in the story. The story also deals with the idea of the scaffold, which is used as a sort of connection between the physical world and the spiritual world.

Variants
This story appears in slightly different variants in different versions. In one version, the young men are out hunting for ducks, and are visited by the spirits of their dead mothers. In another version, the spirits of the dead fathers give the young men a sacred pipe, which they are to keep and use in the proper way.

Suddenly they heard a great noise and the water near them turned bright red. Then they saw a great big fish leap into the air and turn several times over its head. It was a sea monster, Hulahula, the Indians called it. The young men ran away to hide and the monster dived again and again, turning red every time it came out of the water.
In the morning the young men told the others about it and they all went down to the river to see. When the monster came up and turned over its head, they all shouted and threw stones at it. Then it dived again and again, and every time it came out of the water it was red all over.
After a long time it did not come anymore, and the Indians were glad. They made a big feast and danced all night. They said the Hulahula was dead and their chief would be the greatest of all the tribes. But the next year, when the young men went to hunt seals, the Hulahula was there again. It was always there, as long as there were seals in the river.

The legend
This is the story of the Hulahula monster from the Kwakiutl tribe living in the Pacific Northwest. The legend is told by the ethnologist James A. Teit in his 1910 work "The Kwakiutl Laws of Visitation". The story is part of a larger myth cycle that describes a supernatural being known as the Transformer.

Analysis
The story of the Hulahula monster can be analyzed from several angles. From a linguistic point of view, the word Hulahula can be broken down into two parts: Hula meaning "red" and Hula meaning "fish". This suggests that the monster was a red-colored fish. From a mythological perspective, the story describes the encounter with a sea serpent. The legend can also be seen from a sociological point of view. The story describes a feast and a dance that was held in honor of the Transformer. The myths of the Kwakiutl tribes are closely connected to their social structure. The myths describe the laws of visitation, which regulate the exchange of potlatches between tribes. The Hulahula myth describes such a potlatch and the distribution of wealth.

Suddenly they heard a voice: "Klewatam! Klowatam! Klowatam!" It was the voice of the River-man calling from the water. The young men were terrified. They ran home to Egulac and told what had happened.

The River-man (or River Spirit) is a story-telling character in the mythology of the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast of North America. The story is found in variations among the Nuu-chah-nulth, or Nootka, people.

Story
The young men told their chief what had happened, and the chief decided to go down to the river to find out what the River-man wanted. The chief and a number of other men went down to the river, and heard the voice of the River-man as before. The chief called out to the River-man and asked why he did not appear. The River-man came up to the bank and spoke to the chief.
He said: "I am the River-man. I am the keeper of all the fish in the sea. I am the one who sends the fish up the rivers to spawn, and I am the one who sends them back down again. I have heard that your people are not prospering as they once did, and that you do not have as many fish as you once had. I have come to help you. Every year at this time, I will send a great run of fish up your river, and your people shall never starve again."
The chief thanked the River-man, and from that time forward the people of Egulac had plenty of fish.

Variants
There are other variants of this story. In one version, the River-man offers to give the people of Egulac a "great gift". The chief asks what the gift is, and the River-man says that he will give them a "red face". The people of Egulac are terrified, and ask what a "red face" is. The River-man says that it is a face that will make them rich. When the people see the face, they are amazed, for it is the face of a salmon.
